a82.speaker: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, President of Namibia
a82.speech: Urged former Heads of Mission to use their international experience and networks to support Namibia's development agenda.

a82.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a82.speech: Said he is hopeful that the message of unity, inclusivity and shared prosperity championed by the late President Hage Geingob will continue to resonate as Namibians put in the hard work to build a better Namibia.

a82.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a82.speech: Expressed concern over the ongoing situation in the Democratic Republic of Congo, warning that it could escalate beyond its borders and affect the entire region.

a82.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a82.speech: Urged political parties to be exemplary in their conduct as the nation approaches elections ; said the unity and stability in the country are to the benefit of every citizen, irrespective of their political party membership.

a82.speaker: Alka Bhatia, UNDP Resident Representative to Namibia
a82.speech: Says Namibia's development priorities are the same as those of the UN, and that these are aligned with the UNDP country programme.

a82.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a82.speech: Reiterated that any proposal for development projects is welcome, but said discussions must first be exhausted at the line ministries before reaching the State House.

a82.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a82.speech: Called for professional partnerships between Namibian businesses and Chinese counterparts in the health sector.

a82.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a82.speech: Applauded Germany's commitment to the realisation of the Green Hydrogen project and programme in Namibia.

a82.speaker: Sustjie Mbumba, First Lady of Namibia
a82.speech: During the opening of a high-level roundtable discussion on inequalities, HIV, TB, Malaria and Pandemics, encouraged individuals and organisations to speak out against inequality or injustice.

a228.speaker: Chadian authorities
a228.speech: Quite rightly pointed out that the NGO should have complied with Chad's own adoption laws ; the Chadians noted that most of these Sudanese orphans were neither orphans, nor were they from Sudan; they were local kids lured in by Zoe's Ark's false promises of a trip to the clinic or a better school.

a228.speaker: UN agencies and the Red Cross
a228.speech: Subsequently confirmed that most of the children were neither orphans nor from Sudan.

a228.speaker: Court in Chad (court record)
a228.speech: A court in Chad sentenced members of the group to eight years in prison, and ordered them to pay 6.3 million euros in damages to parents of the children.

a228.speaker: Le Figaro
a228.speech: According to Le Figaro, Breteau has given up his ideals, instead running a guesthouse and obtaining his pilot's licence, while Lelouche founded a performance group called the Compagnie Kalahari.

a228.speaker: Emilie Lelouche, partner of Zoe's Ark chairman Eric Breteau (non-response)
a228.speech: The Daily Maverick attempted to contact the pair for comment, but Emilie Lelouche did not answer her cellphone, and has told other media that she is not speaking to anyone about the issue.

a228.speaker: Department of Justice (South Africa)
a228.speech: According to the Department of Justice, there is no extradition treaty in force between South Africa and France.

a228.speaker: Jean-Francois Tavira, pilot recruited by Zoe's Ark to fly the plane
a228.speech: "Breteau is an idealist, ready put everyone in the merde," said Jean-Francois Tavira.

a228.speaker: Presiding judge at the Paris trial
a228.speech: Described the pair's absence as an act of "grand cowardice".

a280.speaker: Callixte Kavuro, Postdoctoral Research Fellow in Public Law, Stellenbosch University
a280.speech: Writes that South Africa's Covid-19 relief measures, and constitutional socio-economic protections in general, need to be harmonised with the Refugees Act to promote access by formally recognised refugees to state relief programmes ; "The interests of asylum seekers, who are not fully protected by the act, also need to be considered as they too have socio-economic rights."

a280.speaker: Callixte Kavuro (study on socio-economic rights of refugees and asylum seekers during the pandemic)
a280.speech: "My study examined the protection of the socio-economic rights of refugees and asylum seekers in the country during the pandemic. It also considered the impact of non-citizenship on the protection of these vulnerable people." ; "I found that although refugees and asylum seekers are protected in law, this is not always the case in practice. Asylum seekers' interests are rarely considered when it comes to socio-economic protections. They must fend for themselves."

a280.speaker: Callixte Kavuro, Postdoctoral Research Fellow in Public Law, Stellenbosch University
a280.speech: Concludes that the South African government has, over the years, displayed an ambivalent attitude towards the protection of refugees and asylum seekers, evident in its adoption of socio-economic laws which do not speak to the Refugees Act, and that this ambivalence stems from the notion among some within government that most asylum seekers and refugees are not "genuine"; "That's why the government did not fully meet its commitment to treat refugees and asylum seekers with dignity and humanity."

a280.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a280.speech: On 15 March 2020 stated that his cabinet was finalising a comprehensive package of interventions to mitigate the expected impact of Covid-19 on the economy, and that such interventions would prioritise protecting the health and well-being of "all South Africans".

a280.speaker: 2019 UN report
a280.speech: According to the report, the country had 89,285 formally recognised refugees and 188,285 asylum seekers.

a280.speaker: Scalabrini Centre (NGO, in litigation)
a280.speech: Successfully argued that the exclusion of asylum seekers from the R350 Social Relief of Distress grant was arbitrary and unreasonable, and that it also violated their constitutional rights to equality, dignity and access to social security.

a280.speaker: Department of Employment and Labour
a280.speech: Argued that its computer system was not designed to capture the numbers appearing on the refugees and asylum seekers' status permits.

a280.speaker: Equality Court (2017 order)
a280.speech: Ordered the department in 2017 to fix its computer system to capture the numbers appearing on refugees' and asylum seekers' status permits.

a289.speaker: 2018 Global Food Policy Report
a289.speech: States that African countries should continue to monitor progress toward the Malabo Declaration on Accelerated Agricultural Growth and Transformation for Shared Prosperity and Improved Livelihoods, while engaging with regional commitments on environmental health.

a289.speaker: 2018 Global Food Policy Report
a289.speech: States that country-level leadership and champions who work to end hunger and malnutrition are among the most important drivers of change, citing encouraging campaigns including China's commitment to achieving Healthy China 2030 and Ethiopia's Seqota Declaration on ending undernutrition by 2030.

a289.speaker: 2018 Global Food Policy Report
a289.speech: Underlines that in the face of economic slowdown and a decline in export revenues, attracting Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) becomes critical to sustaining economic recovery ; findings show that FDI flows to Africa decreased by 3 percent in 2016 to USD 59 billion, with over half of total FDI directed to five countries: Angola, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana and Nigeria; Egypt's increase of 17 percent reflects the discovery of gas reserves, while the 28 percent decline in the Democratic Republic of the Congo followed the sharp fall of global metals prices ; points out that in East Africa FDI to Ethiopia increased by 46 percent with rising investment in manufacturing and infrastructure, and that in West Africa FDI grew by 12 percent, boosted by increased investment in oil and other natural resources in Nigeria and Ghana.

a289.speaker: 2018 Global Food Policy Report
a289.speech: Points out that continued poor rains in parts of Ethiopia, Kenya and Somalia in late 2016 and early 2017 caused a major food security crisis, particularly in Somalia and Ethiopia, that as of December 2017 emergency conditions were expected to continue in parts of the region into 2018, and that the drought has significantly impacted agricultural and pastoral livelihoods in the Horn of Africa, with sustained humanitarian assistance likely to be needed.

a289.speaker: 2018 Global Food Policy Report
a289.speech: States that, although agricultural research spending and human resource capacity in Africa south of the Sahara have grown considerably, this growth has been uneven and trends are driven by large countries such as Ethiopia, Nigeria and South Africa; "Many countries are overly dependent on volatile and unsustainable donor funds."

a328.speaker: Gambians Against Looted Assets (GALA)
a328.speech: Says they remain steadfast in their plan to protest on Thursday, May 8, despite ongoing discussions with the Gambia Police Force’s Interpol Unit ; announced today that it underwent a screening at 17:00 GMT at the Interpol Office after submitting a permit request to the Office of the Inspector General of Police (IGP) ; “Whether 20 people or 2,000 people, we will protest on Thursday, with or without a permit.”

a328.speaker: Interpol officials, Gambia Police Force
a328.speech: During the screening, questioned the motive behind the protest and raised unspecified security concerns; the police promised to advise the IGP and provide a response.

a328.speaker: Madi Jobarteh, Executive Director of the Edward Francis Small Center for Rights and Justice
a328.speech: Sharply criticized the police’s stance: “The Gambia Police Force has no reason to question the motive of citizens who wish to protest. Protest is not a crime, and protesters are not criminals” ; argued that the police’s role is to ensure security for citizens exercising their constitutional right to assembly, not to obstruct it ; challenged the police to substantiate their security concerns, pointing out the absence of reported threats from the Gambia Police Force, National Intelligence Agency, Gambia Armed Forces, or National Security Advisor since January 2025.

a328.speaker: Madi Jobarteh, Executive Director of the Edward Francis Small Center for Rights and Justice
a328.speech: Highlighted recent large-scale public events, such as the Independence Day celebrations on February 18 and May Day Sports on May 1, held near the State House without incident, and noted President Adama Barrow’s recent nationwide tour, which proceeded smoothly. “The Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Information have declared The Gambia’s security situation as unparalleled in the sub-region” ; “What security concerns is the Gambia Police talking about?”

a328.speaker: Madi Jobarteh, Executive Director of the Edward Francis Small Center for Rights and Justice
a328.speech: Urged the IGP to uphold the Constitution and grant GALA’s permit, emphasizing that the right to protest is a fundamental entitlement. “The IGP must respect and protect this entrenched constitutional right.”

a328.speaker: Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Information of The Gambia
a328.speech: Have declared The Gambia’s security situation as unparalleled in the sub-region (as cited by Madi Jobarteh).

a450.speaker: Economic experts
a450.speech: According to economic experts, strong diplomatic relations encourage trade agreements that will reduce tariffs and barriers, making it easy for businesses to operate across borders, boosting exports, imports and foreign direct investment and hence stimulating the country’s economic growth.

a450.speaker: Available data (cited)
a450.speech: According to the available data, in the 2021–2024 periods, Finland allocated approximately EUR 56 million to Tanzania, emphasising democracy, gender equality and sustainable forest-based livelihoods.

a450.speaker: Thereza Zitting, Ambassador of Finland to Tanzania
a450.speech: Said the existing relationship between the two countries has been characterized by collaborative efforts in development cooperation, trade, governance and cultural exchange ; said Finland has been a consistent development partner for Tanzania, focusing on sectors such as forestry, education, and good governance ; said both nations have expressed a desire to enhance mutual trade and investments and insisted that Finland will continue strengthening cooperation with Tanzania, particularly in economic development and environmental conservation, with a focus on tree planting and forest conservation ; expressed her satisfaction with the continued bilateral cooperation, clarifying that while some countries have severed diplomatic ties due to various reasons, Tanzania and Finland have remained committed to their partnership.

a450.speaker: Thereza Zitting, Ambassador of Finland to Tanzania
a450.speech: Praised President Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan for her efforts in strengthening economic diplomacy and bilateral relations, citing the recent energy summit held in Dar es Salaam: “The summit was one of the best organised in the country. I see the President’s initiative in clean cooking yielding positive results” ; highlighted that President Samia’s initiatives in promoting clean cooking energy have greatly benefited Tanzanians, especially women, by reducing health and safety risks associated with traditional cooking methods: “I saw this as a crucial initiative to support women, who face significant risks when cooking at home” ; explained that the initiative will also contribute to environmental conservation by reducing reliance on firewood for cooking, which leads to deforestation, emphasising that Finland and Tanzania’s cooperation in forestry remains strong and sustainable ; “At the moment, we are working closely on forest conservation—keeping forests green, healthy, and viable… we are promoting gender equality by encouraging women’s participation in economic and political life”.

a450.speaker: Thereza Zitting, Ambassador of Finland to Tanzania
a450.speech: “One of our successes is the cooperation between civil society organisations, in addition to government-to-government collaborations” ; noted that both countries are placing increased emphasis on private sector collaboration and are exploring new forms of cooperation, such as city-to-city partnerships, highlighting the longstanding cooperation between Tampere City in Finland and MCC in Mwanza: “I was happy to hear that the partnership between Tampere City and Mwanza City Council has existed since 1988. Over the years, they have engaged in various twinning activities” ; noted that last year both cities collaborated with UN-Habitat to explore ways to implement SDGs together: “This is significant work, and while much has been achieved, there is still more to do. We will continue to explore the best ways to collaborate” ; emphasized that the partnership has been particularly successful in the areas of education and infrastructure, reaffirming Finland’s strong friendship with Tanzania: “My wish for the Tanzanian people is to continue this valuable cooperation. We have many opportunities to work together in the future”.

a450.speaker: Said Mtanda, Mwanza Regional Commissioner
a450.speech: Invited Finland to invest in modern fish farming in Mwanza City, citing the availability of water infrastructure for the farming, explaining that more than 53 per cent of the city’s area is surrounded by the waters of Lake Victoria ; praised the Finland government for the support it had been offering in the country especially in the area of education, environment conservation and technology, promising to enhance the existing cooperation between the two countries.

a450.speaker: Sima Constantino, Mayor of Mwanza City Council (MCC)
a450.speech: Said the council is committed to translating those collaborative efforts into tangible benefits for the community by integrating social, economic, political and cultural development initiatives ; expressed appreciation for the support and mentorship provided by Tampere City in SDG localisation ; noted that past projects under the Tampere-Mwanza sister city cooperation have had a positive impact on the environment, education and good governance: “As Mwanza City Council we are privileged to pioneer SDG localisation, setting an example for other cities in Tanzania following our first local SDG review” ; acknowledged the role of UN-Habitat in funding Mwanza’s first voluntary local review and facilitating the city’s participation in international platforms: “The new city strategy adopted in 2023 by Tampere City, along with our Mwanza City strategic plan, has allowed us to align our development goals with the SDGs”.

a450.speaker: Jeremaya Luberege, Acting MCC Director
a450.speech: Highlighted the council’s achievements in SDG implementation, particularly in creating a better working environment for staff, improving healthcare facilities and advancing the education sector.

a450.speaker: Amin Abadallah, Mwanza-Tampere Cooperation Project Coordinator
a450.speech: Said MCC has gained more benefit after adopting a voluntary local review of progress on the SDGs that is undertaken by local and regional governments to foster SDG localisation and demonstrate local governments’ capacity and commitments ; explained that the cities of Mwanza and Tampere joined their efforts under the North South Local Government Cooperation Programme since the beginning of 2002, with the history of their cooperation going back to 1988 when they became twin sister cities: “The cooperation project has engaged in supporting development projects and capacity building of Mwanza city ensuring the improvement of service delivery by supporting good governance, environmental conservation, school cooperation, Fire Prevention Emergency Unit and University Cooperation” ; said that in October 2022 the two cities established a two-way collaboration to drive implementation of the SDGs and monitor progress through Mwanza’s Voluntary Local Review, signing a memorandum of understanding with UN-Habitat ; “One of its benefits is raising awareness and educating citizens and stakeholders about the SDGs and their relevance for local development and influencing national and international policymaking to ensure that the SDGs reflect local needs and priorities”.

a539.speaker: Moussa Diarra, secretary general of the UNTM-SECMIMA Union Committee of Fekola S.A - B2Gold
a539.speech: Announced at a press briefing the filing of a strike notice dated 10 November 2024, with the work stoppage running from Friday 29 November at 00:00 until 5 December 2024 at 23:59, a total of 168 hours ; said the work stoppage results from the failure of negotiations with management, which remains inflexible in the face of the union's demands, and denounced in particular a wave of disciplinary proceedings and sanctions against employees and the continued deterioration of the social climate, aggravated by the behaviour of the head of the Human Resources department and of the quarry manager, accused of undermining efforts towards constructive social dialogue.

a539.speaker: UNTM-SECMIMA Union Committee of Fekola S.A - B2Gold (formal demands)
a539.speech: Sets out the following requirements: the launch of an internal investigation into cases of employment using dubious identities in order to establish responsibilities and sanction those involved; the immediate and unconditional cancellation of all disciplinary proceedings and sanctions brought against employees; the immediate and unconditional lifting of the contract suspensions of union members; an end to harassment and constraints forcing employees to work in the underground mine without prior agreement between the two parties; and strict respect for freedom of association in accordance with workers' rights.

a601.speaker: US Agency for International Development (USAID) (program announcement)
a601.speech: Announced that it is accepting new applications for the Development Innovation Ventures (DIV) program, that anyone, anywhere can apply at any time, and set out the tiered funding stages and separate evidence grants; stated that since 2010, DIV has invested in over 190 solutions across 46 countries and all sectors in which USAID invests, has directly affected more than 30 million lives, that over half of DIV grantees had never received USAID funding before, and that DIV has mobilized USD4.60 of external funding for every USD1 from the American people.

a815.speaker: Richard Msowoya, Chief of the delegation of the SADC Election Observation Mission (SEOM) for Tanzania and former Speaker of the Malawi National Assembly
a815.speech: Stated that SADC is participating in the election observation exercise at the invitation of the Tanzanian government; emphasized that the mission will adhere to international standards, regional guidelines, and ethical principles to ensure that the election is free and fair; noted that Tanzania is the third country in the SADC region to hold a general election within one month, following peaceful elections in Malawi and Seychelles, which he said demonstrates regional solidarity in strengthening democracy; added that since the arrival of the SEOM team in Tanzania the mission has observed that election campaigns by various political parties are ongoing peacefully, indicating Tanzania’s maturity in promoting and upholding democratic principles; outlined key criteria that will be used to assess the election process, including citizen participation, respect for human rights and freedoms, equal access for political parties to media platforms, and the presence of a peaceful, non-threatening, and non-discriminatory environment, as well as the integrity of electoral institutions and the legal framework, voter education and civic awareness, the freedom to contest and vote, and the importance of accepting and respecting election results.

a815.speaker: Said Shaib Mussa, Deputy Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and East African Cooperation
a815.speech: Said that the involvement of international observers helps promote transparency, fairness, and justice in the electoral process, thereby strengthening democracy among SADC member states.

a903.speaker: Mariatou Koné, Minister of National Education and Literacy of Côte d’Ivoire
a903.speech: “I am here for two main reasons: to encourage you and congratulate you for your daily commitment, but also to listen to your concerns and integrate your ideas into our joint actions” ; she recalled the strategic importance of these actors in the management of educational resources: “You play a key role. If your management fails, the whole system suffers, with a direct impact on the learning conditions of pupils.”

a903.speaker: KONÉ Ouokan, President of the AAAC-CI, and ZEBA Germaine, President of the ANIE-CI
a903.speech: Expressed their satisfaction: “Since our creation in 1996, this is the first time a minister has received us. You value us and your leadership inspires us to build a quality school.”

a903.speaker: DAHO Abdrahmane, Director of Financial Affairs
a903.speech: Also welcomed this initiative: “Your leadership is a benchmark. This meeting is an opportunity to benefit from your guidance.”

a903.speaker: Participants (bursars and accounting assistants)
a903.speech: Renewed their support for the Minister’s vision, stating: “We remain at your side to overcome the obstacles and build a high-performing school.”

a994.speaker: Youssouf Sylla, author of “Réflexion sur l’autonomie stratégique africaine” (L’Harmattan)
a994.speech: On why Africa needs strategic autonomy: said that defended by France in 1994 in the Defence White Paper, the concept of strategic autonomy has become a major European ambition since the ongoing disengagement of the second Trump administration from Europe, because “for Europe, the historic American ally is no longer reliable.” But strategic debate cannot be the preserve of Europe alone: Africa must take ownership of the concept if it wants to become a continent that counts. African strategic autonomy covers three interdependent and integrated pillars - political, security and economic - and within the African Union, Agenda 2063 has since 2013 carried the vision of an integrated, prosperous and peaceful Africa driven by its own citizens.

a994.speaker: Youssouf Sylla, author of “Réflexion sur l’autonomie stratégique africaine” (L’Harmattan)
a994.speech: On the four reasons that justify African strategic autonomy: first, the need to break Africa’s almost mechanical alignment with the positions of external powers, as seen in the mini break-up of ECOWAS with the withdrawal of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, and in the continent’s UN vote of March 2022 on the Ukrainian crisis; second, the need to end Africa’s excessive or chronic dependence on foreign aid, noting that Macky Sall and Mahamat Faki begged President Putin in June 2022 to lift the Black Sea blockade, and that Donald Trump’s recent decrees withdrawing the United States from the WHO and the Paris Climate Agreement, closing USAID offices in Africa, and the risk of non-renewal of AGOA “risk causing the collapse of certain health systems on the continent and aggravating economic, humanitarian and ecological crises there”; third, the rise and normalisation of far-right parties in the West, whose contempt for Africa should lead them to turn away from the continent and reduce or eliminate official development assistance; fourth, the relocation to Africa of rivalries between international powers, especially in unstable countries such as Mali, Sudan, Libya and the DRC. Warned that “without decisive action by African leaders, the continent’s vulnerabilities will only grow with time, to the point of making it, once again, the losing party in the geopolitical shifts now under way.”

a994.speaker: Youssouf Sylla, author of “Réflexion sur l’autonomie stratégique africaine” (L’Harmattan)
a994.speech: On how to build strategic autonomy in practice: said any generalisation would be imprudent, that Africa is not a homogeneous but a heterogeneous entity - leading some specialists to speak not of one Africa but of several Africas - and that realising Agenda 2063 is a gigantic challenge depending above all on the political will of the heads of state and government of the African Union, which is “the fuel that will set in motion the machine for building the economic, political and security pillars of African strategic autonomy.” Only when they commit, in an integrated approach, to the three pillars will Africa be able to speak with one voice and take a credible place alongside other powers: “The work is certainly titanic, but not impossible to accomplish. Other countries have already taken this difficult road. Why would African states not do so?”

a994.speaker: Andriy Yusov, spokesperson for Kyiv’s military intelligence service
a994.speech: Admitted on Ukrainian television in July 2024 that the information supplied by Ukraine to the separatists of northern Mali allowed them to inflict, at Tinzaouaten, enormous losses of human life on Malian soldiers and on the Russian fighters of the Africa Corps, formerly Wagner.

a994.speaker: Economist Intelligence Unit report (2022)
a994.speech: According to the report, about 7 African countries live under a democratic regime - Mauritius, Botswana, South Africa, Namibia, Ghana, Cape Verde and Lesotho - while the others are either in a hybrid system (half-democratic, half-authoritarian) or in an authoritarian system.

a1033.speaker: Mozambican government
a1033.speech: has thanked Spain for its assistance in the fight against terrorism in Cabo Delgado, materialised through humanitarian assistance, as well as for Spain's contribution to the European Union Military Training Mission (EUTM Moz).

a1033.speaker: José Manuel Albares, Spain's Minister of Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation (post on X/Twitter)
a1033.speech: “I receive in Madrid my Mozambican counterpart, Verónica Macamo. We have reviewed our political, economic, educational, cultural and cooperation relations, and agreed to continue deepening them. Spain is committed to the stability and prosperity of Mozambique and Africa.”

a1048.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, South African President
a1048.speech: During a business conference in Johannesburg on Thursday, expressed his desire for improved diplomatic ties after Trump's executive order targeting South Africa's land reform policies, and noted the importance of reaching "a meaningful deal" with the US to address various issues impacting bilateral relations: "We want to go and do a meaningful deal with the United States on a whole range of issues."

a1048.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, South African President
a1048.speech: Defended South Africa's land reform initiative, asserting that it is constitutional and aimed at rectifying historical injustices from apartheid; refuted claims that current laws allow for arbitrary land seizures, assuring that expropriation would be conducted fairly.

a1131.speaker: Vera Kamtukule, Malawi Tourism Minister
a1131.speech: Urged stakeholders in the tourism industry to plan for any potential impact that may arise following the suspension of United States Agency for International Development (USaid)-funded programmes in the country; said tourism industry players need to plan for how to address the impact of this move on the sector: "What are we doing about that? Have we considered how this will affect tourism? How are we positioning ourselves to stand against it? These are the conversations we need to have, so that when the impact comes, we should be able to counter it." ; She also challenged tourism industry players to ensure quality in the services they provide.

a1131.speaker: Cuthbert Simphiwe Ncube, African Tourism Board Executive Chairman
a1131.speech: Said that there is a need to change the current narrative surrounding tourism in Africa: "We think tourism is about white-collar work, but we need to change that perception. We should start to say, 'Wow, our brothers and sisters, we can even start appreciating the tourism industry domestically or regionally.'" ; He added that the tourism industry is crucial to the economic growth of both Malawi and the continent as a whole.

a1131.speaker: Justin Dzinkambani, Malawi Tourism Council Chairperson
a1131.speech: Stressed that embracing local and continental tourism is crucial to minimising the impact of the possible withdrawal of USaid staff from Malawi: "We should treat this as a disaster, and we need to start working on strategies that can help the tourism sector. For me, I see local tourism as one of the sectors to focus on and at the same time, the African Tourism global partnership is a key component."

a1131.speaker: Chifuno Stevens, Dedza Pottery General Manager, training participant
a1131.speech: Said she expected to learn a great deal through the training.

a1141.speaker: Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC)
a1141.speech: Directed producers and refiners to provide the commission with cargo price quotes on crude supply and delivery for effective monitoring and regulation of transactions among parties. NUPRC said in a statement it could not allow pricing to impede domestic refining.

a1141.speaker: Gbenga Komolafe, NUPRC chief (statement)
a1141.speech: Said the meeting agreed to concede to a framework that would be mutually beneficial to ensure that local refineries were not strangulated due to off-the-curve prices. Mr Komolafe said the meeting was focused on the status review of the Framework for Seamless Operationalisation of Domestic Crude Oil Supply Obligation Template.

a1141.speaker: Gbenga Komolafe, NUPRC chief
a1141.speech: "We will never allow price strangulation to disincentivise our domestic refining capacity optimisation" ; He said the regulator would work to ensure there was no "crude supply profiteering," although he also said it did not condone any loss-making in oil production ; "The regulator does not support cost under-recovery in the upstream sector, and we will continue to work to ensure that crude supply profiteering as a negative factor that can strangulate our domestic refining capacity optimisation is disallowed."

a1141.speaker: Gbenga Komolafe, NUPRC chief
a1141.speech: To ensure transparency, Komolafe requested monthly cargo price quotes on crude oil supply and delivery from both producers and refiners and said it was up to the regulator to balance upstream development with a sustainable domestic energy supply chain. "We need to have the price quotes monthly," he directed. "We allow all our processes to be transparent. While the Federal Government targets the implementation of the regulation, all parties must submit to the rules of engagement as a guide for operation."

a1141.speaker: Gbenga Komolafe, NUPRC chief
a1141.speech: Said the Federal Government and crude oil producers in Nigeria had committed to working toward a sustainable supply of crude oil to local refineries under a market-determined pricing system, the aim being to ensure that while the operators do business optimally, the refineries are not starved of feedstock. He said it was part of efforts to effectively implement key sections of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) 2021, especially the issue of pricing and crude supply to the domestic refineries. According to him, President Bola Tinubu is fully committed to providing a level playing ground for producers and refiners to do business in the industry.

a1141.speaker: Gbenga Komolafe, NUPRC chief
a1141.speech: Assured that NUPRC would continue attracting the needed investments to boost upstream development and optimise hydrocarbon resources for sustainability of domestic energy supply in the midstream and downstream sector.

a1141.speaker: Dangote Refinery
a1141.speech: Complained that oil majors were hindering local crude purchases by demanding excessive premiums or saying they had no available supplies.

a1148.speaker: Henok Mehari, musician, founder of the Mehari Brothers band and host of the Musicology programme
a1148.speech: Says that he shifted to DStv because it was the only choice he had after resigning from Kana. Even though Henok knew that he might lose some viewers after leaving Kana, he thinks it is a step in the right direction, supposing that pay-TV outweighs the drawbacks of losing viewership for artists like him. The pay-TV system is not harmful, according to Henok, who argues that it is a tool that will help elevate art to the level it deserves in a country where artists have a difficult time gaining recognition and monetising their work. "After a certain period of time and coordination, it is clear that the Ethiopian TV industry is going to shift to the scheme of pay-TV because our art also needs the growth we see in other nations."

a1148.speaker: Viewers of the Musicology programme
a1148.speech: Argue that they will not have the access they were used to once the show begins airing on a pay-TV platform requiring them to pay a monthly subscription fee.

a1148.speaker: Management at MultiChoice Ethiopia Plc
a1148.speech: Were reluctant to say just how much the service has grown.

a1148.speaker: techcentral.co.za, South African technology news website
a1148.speech: MultiChoice had around 19 million subscribers across Africa at the end of 2019, with the majority being from South Africa.

a1148.speaker: Biruk Gebru, CEO of Bridgetech Broadcasting and Media Plc
a1148.speech: StarTimes is a China-based broadcaster that came to Ethiopia in 2018 in anticipation of a large market in the pay-TV industry. "Currently, our big customers are families with kids, documentary lovers, and sports fans."

a1148.speaker: Biruk Gebru, CEO of Bridgetech Broadcasting and Media Plc
a1148.speech: "Even with the problems, the market is untapped and new players are welcome" ; "Local content is the magical formula for any pay-TV operator in the world" ; An estimated seven million households in Ethiopia have at least one television set and about 55pc of the population has partial access to television, but only five percent of the households that have access are subscribed to pay-TV services, according to Biruk.

a1148.speaker: Teodros Abraham, CEO of Bruh Entertainment
a1148.speech: "We wanted to bring something different to the community" ; "For the moment, we have bought hundreds of local movies but we have plans to produce and co-produce new programmes as well" ; "What actually matters is the content and creating a platform where local creative-space companies can be motivated."

a1148.speaker: Officials from the Ethiopian Media Authority
a1148.speech: Said the new media law passed earlier this year has brought with it some motivational aspects, including recommending tax reductions, investment incentives like giving working space and loans, and including the broadcasters in the foreign currency supply chain.

a1148.speaker: Ezana Wubishet, communication and PR manager at MultiChoice Ethiopia
a1148.speech: According to Ezana, they initiated the process of including Ethiopian content programmes early on but the implementation took time because they had to do their research and produce the quality and premium programming they were aiming for. They are working with more than 30 producers to create new content.

a1148.speaker: Ayele Ashebir, technician of Ayu Dish
a1148.speech: According to Ayele, most of their current work consists of adjusting satellites for Ethiosat, and even that is not to a great extent.

a1148.speaker: Satellite dish installers
a1148.speech: Are claiming that the impact pay-TV is having on their business is minimal.

a1148.speaker: Yared Kassa, training coordinator at Tom Videography and Photography Training Centre
a1148.speech: According to Yared, the fact that foreign movies are being dubbed in Amharic by pay-TV service providers has both positive and negative effects. The negative effects include drawing the attention of the audience completely to foreign art products and smothering the local industry, which is still in its infancy. However, it also shows local art professionals what the audience needs and what standards they should follow. "They are a very loud alarm for the country's art industry" ; He believes that even if pay-TV has limited reach in the country, the platforms are beneficial in that they are unveiling Ethiopia's art industry, along with the culture, to other places. "Pay-TV will modernise art, along with its professionals, and that will lead to its acceptance as a normal commodity."

a1222.speaker: United Nations
a1222.speech: Warns that northern Mozambique experienced a "deepening" humanitarian crisis in June, caused by funding shortages, natural disasters and escalating armed violence in Cabo Delgado province.

a1222.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a1222.speech: "Escalation of violence by non-state armed groups (NSAG) continued to drive displacement, disrupt essential services, severely restrict movement, exacerbate food insecurity, and impede the delivery of life-saving assistance." ; "on 24 June, 568 individuals, including 324 children, fled NSAG attacks in Quinto Congresso village towards the already overcrowded Macomia district headquarters," bringing "the total number of people displaced by conflict to 48,000 since 1 January," many urgently requiring food, shelter, necessities and drinking water. ; "The conflict continues to impact the protection needs of people. In early 2025, Cabo Delgado saw a 22 per cent rise in reported GBV cases compared to 2024, due to improved reporting and growing awareness but also underscores the gender-specific impact of the conflict."

a1222.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a1222.speech: Added that the government have facilitated returns in Macomia, Metuge, and Montepuez in Cabo Delgado, and recently in Mecula, Niassa, "largely driven by inadequate humanitarian assistance and overcrowding in IDP sites" ; "the returnees have found nothing in their areas of origin as their homes, agricultural plots and livelihoods were destroyed and basic services have not been restored" ; "Those who opted for resettlement found the proposed sites lacking in essential services. The lack of response to returns heightens vulnerabilities and protection risks."

a1222.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a1222.speech: Pointed to persistent "post-cyclone needs and gaps," explaining that, with funding constraints, people affected by the three cyclones still require adequate assistance. "The first assessments conducted since March in Lalaua and Muecate districts in Nampula revealed that a combined 70,000 people were affected by the cyclones but have not received assistance since March."

a1222.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a1222.speech: Highlights an opportunity: humanitarian funding could rise again after a 26% decline between 2024 and 2025, from $74 million (€62.8 million) to $55 million (€46.7m). "As a result, some 260,000 people are left without access to WASH services while 200,000 people remain without adequate shelter and NFIs. In addition, the laboratory sample collection program, serving 250,000 individuals monthly, primarily those with HIV and TB, has been abruptly halted."

a1222.speaker: OCHA Mozambique (@MozambiqueOcha), social media post, 8 July 2025
a1222.speech: "Crisis in Northern Mozambique, as of June 2025: Funding down by 26%; 260K pple lack WASH services; 200K need shelter; High protection risks, ongoing displacement; Food aid progress in C. Delgado, but urgent support still needed."

a1222.speaker: OCHA Mozambique (@MozambiqueOcha), social media post, 3 July 2025
a1222.speech: "Humanitarian response in facing critical challenges! While 862K people in C. Delgado received aid, this is 8.1% decline from 2024. Funding down 25.4%; Partners decreased by 36.4%; 1.3M conflict-affected people urgently need support."

a1222.speaker: OCHA Mozambique (@MozambiqueOcha), social media post, 13 June 2025
a1222.speech: "In Mozambique, a complex humanitarian crisis continues: 609K remain displaced in the north; Over 700K people have returned home; Returnees face critical shortages in education, health & basic services; Cash aid is reaching remote communities, offering vital support."

a1288.speaker: Mozambican government / Ministry of Finance (document on budget execution for the first half of the year)
a1288.speech: acknowledges that the end of funding for projects in Mozambique, from the US agency USAID, "represented a significant external shock", with impacts on health, agriculture and employment, and threatening the "collapse" of basic services; the suspension of funding in January, and its subsequent closure, forced it to "redirect internal resources to prevent the collapse of basic services". ; "In this context, the government has adopted policy measures aimed at ensuring the sustainability of essential services and stimulating the national economy" ; "These measures include redirecting public spending, mobilizing domestic resources, supporting domestic production, strengthening social protection and improving efficiency in budget management, thus mitigating the negative impacts of the interruption of foreign aid and promoting the country's economic and social resilience".

a1288.speaker: Fitch (ratings agency)
a1288.speech: acknowledges that the suspension of USAID support to Mozambique also had an impact on the shortage of foreign currency which is felt in Mozambique and represents 3% of Mozambican GDP. "The shortage of foreign currency increased in 2025, partly due to the decline in external disbursements to the government and the suspension of USAID," Fitch writes in its most recent rating assessment for the country, highlighting that the US agency disbursed support to Mozambique of US$586 million (€505 million) in 2024, primarily for projects related to health and education, "equivalent to 3% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP)".

a1288.speaker: Mozambican government (July data)
a1288.speech: At least 2,500 jobs were lost in Mozambique with the cut in US foreign aid through USAID, according to July data from the Mozambican government, which admitted it was "a problem" for the economy.

a1288.speaker: Ivete Alane, Mozambican Minister of Labour, Gender and Social Action
a1288.speech: "The last meeting I had with the group created by organizations that benefited from the funding spoke of around 2,500 jobs," noting that there was no "official estimate".

a1322.speaker: President of Turkey (Recep Tayyip Erdogan)
a1322.speech: Requested international assistance in the face of the scale of the tragedy.

a1322.speaker: United Nations (UN)
a1322.speech: Announced a grant of 25 million dollars to help launch the humanitarian response.

a1322.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
a1322.speech: Said that nearly 40 international rescue teams should soon be on the ground to assist Turkish rescuers ; that the UN and its partners are monitoring the situation on the ground, while information flows are limited because of chronic telecommunications disruptions and power cuts.

a1322.speaker: Carsten Hansen, Middle East regional director of the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC)
a1322.speech: "The earthquake struck at the worst hour of the night, at the worst time of the year."

a1322.speaker: International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC)
a1322.speech: Declared that it had observed "significant damage to infrastructure in the governorates of Aleppo, Latakia, Hama and Tartous (in the large cities but also in the countryside). The extent of the damage is being assessed." ; According to its latest figures, 1,509 people have died and 3,548 have been injured, a number expected to rise considerably over the next 24 hours ; Launched a total emergency appeal for 200 million Swiss francs (about 215 million US dollars).

a1322.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a1322.speech: Said the UN was counting on the international community to help the thousands of people affected by the disaster, "many of whom were already in urgent need of humanitarian assistance in areas where access is difficult."

a1360.speaker: Omri Sender, counsel for the State of Israel before the International Court of Justice
a1360.speech: Told the International Court of Justice that South Africa's claims of genocide in Gaza did not meet requirements for urgency and irreparable harm - and that only Israel would suffer harm that could not be reversed if the court granted the interim order SA seeks ; "It falls to me to address the condition of risk of irreparable harm and urgency. This third condition is, of course, dependent on the two preceding ones... It follows that the irreparable consequences cannot, in the present case, be caused by the alleged disregard of rights under the Genocide Convention." ; "the conclusion is that the condition of irreparable prejudice and urgency cannot be met. It is Israel and its citizens who would risk irreparable harm if the Request of South Africa were to be granted."

a1360.speaker: Omri Sender, counsel for the State of Israel before the International Court of Justice
a1360.speech: Argued that the Applicant's factual account is "entirely one-sided" and makes "hardly any mention of the extraordinary efforts undertaken by Israel - and by a host of other States and international actors - to improve the humanitarian situation" ; said Israel has taken "concrete measures aimed specifically at recognizing and ensuring the right" of the group in question to exist, "facilitating the provision of more and more humanitarian assistance for people in need throughout the Gaza Strip", including the re-opening of a dozen bakeries with the capacity to produce more than two million breads a day, an average of 109 food trucks a day over the last two weeks compared with 70 before the war, water supplied by two pipelines and a new pipe from Egypt, four field hospitals and two floating hospitals, 180 000 litres of fuel a day and an average of 90 tonnes of cooking gas per day ; said "A great effort is indeed invested in eliminating bottlenecks so as to improve the entrance and distribution of aid - notwithstanding Hamas constantly stealing it."

a1360.speaker: Omri Sender, counsel for the State of Israel before the International Court of Justice
a1360.speech: Said civilians "have been severely affected by the hostilities instigated by Hamas", whose "systematic strategy of prosecuting war from under, and within, the civilian population exposes civilians to great risk - and it has brought about great suffering", while "Israel has done - and is doing - a great deal to alleviate this suffering in very challenging circumstances."

a1360.speaker: Omri Sender, counsel for the State of Israel before the International Court of Justice
a1360.speech: Said that "the scope and intensity of the hostilities has been decreasing", and that the United Nations Security Council had only recently adopted resolution 2720 for the specific purpose of alleviating the humanitarian situation; contrary to what was heard the previous day, "this resolution does not 'remain unimplemented'. A Senior Coordinator has been appointed and indeed began her work; the Council remains actively seised of the matter." Israel is already working with the Senior Coordinator and has co-ordinated the entrance of a United Nations delegation into northern Gaza.

a1360.speaker: Omri Sender, counsel for the State of Israel before the International Court of Justice
a1360.speech: Said "the lack of urgency within the meaning of the Court's case law is further demonstrated by assurances provided before you today by Israel's Co-Agents", that "Israel remains bound, at all times, by its international legal obligations", and that "your consistent case law suggests that assurances of the kind offered by Israel may well render the indication of provisional measures unnecessary."

a1360.speaker: Professor Malcolm Shaw and Galit Raguan, counsel for Israel
a1360.speech: "have already shown that the provisions relied upon by the Applicant do not afford, even prima facie, a basis on which this Court's jurisdiction could be founded. They also showed that the rights asserted by the Applicant cannot be regarded as plausible."

a1360.speaker: World Food Programme
a1360.speech: "has said that the delivery of flour, salt, sugar and yeast continues, so as to enable more bakeries to re-open, 'increasing accessibility and affordability' for thousands of families."

a1360.speaker: Israel's Defence Minister
a1360.speech: "said last week that Israeli forces would be shifting from the 'intense maneuvering phase of the war' toward 'different types of special operations'." (statement made in an interview to international media, at tab 16-A of the Volume submitted)

a1360.speaker: Spokesperson for the Israeli military
a1360.speech: "confirmed that the Israeli campaign had already started a transition to fewer ground troops and fewer airstrikes. 'The war shifted a stage', he said... he spoke of a new and less intense phase of fighting. He specifically mentioned that Israel will continue to reduce the number of troops in Gaza."

a1360.speaker: United Nations Security Council (resolution 2720 of 22 December 2023)
a1360.speech: "the Council demanded the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, as well as the delivery of humanitarian assistance at scale directly to the Palestinian civilian population throughout the Gaza Strip... the Council requested the Secretary-General to appoint a Senior Coordinator in order to establish a United Nations mechanism for accelerating the provision of humanitarian relief consignments to Gaza."

a1360.speaker: South Africa (the Applicant in the ICJ case)
a1360.speech: "mentioned yesterday the number of trucks entering Gaza each day before and after the war" and argued that Security Council resolution 2720 "remains unimplemented", that the multilateral large-scale humanitarian effort is lacking and that scaling up access of humanitarian relief to Gaza would be of no avail.

a1360.speaker: COGAT, the unit in the Israeli Ministry of Defence in charge of monitoring the humanitarian situation (official data/website)
a1360.speech: Cited as the source for daily updated details concerning the various ongoing humanitarian efforts, including official data that from 8 December the amount of fuel entering Gaza has doubled and currently stands at 180 000 litres a day.

a1360.speaker: Government of Israel (decision of 15 December)
a1360.speech: "Israel decided to open its crossing at Kerem Shalom with the express intention to 'improve and upgrade' the delivery of humanitarian assistance to Palestinian civilians in Gaza."

a1364.speaker: Pedagogical adviser representing the regional inspector, Ali-Sabieh
a1364.speech: Welcomed the participants to the regional inspectorate and recalled that reading is very important insofar as it ensures the acquisition of knowledge and basic skills; the more a pupil reads, the more his or her general culture and communication performance improve. Said the main objectives are first to encourage parents to support their children in mastering reading, and to promote the pleasure of reading in pupils by organising activities around reading at home or at school outside learning hours. Ended his address by stating that it is essential, indeed important, to promote reading in order to give the pupil that feeling, that desire to feed on books and to find in them everything he needs: knowledge and pleasure, comfort, amusement, reflection - in short, creativity.

a1364.speaker: Representative of FHI 360
a1364.speech: Said that this project focuses essentially on the learning of reading in basic school with all its components, and that parents' support for learning - and above all for their children's practice of out-of-school reading - remains the main theme of this workshop. He hammered home to the parents present that without mastery of the act of reading and of the comprehension of texts or passages read there is no learning at school, and that the time pupils spend at school is far less than the time spent at home, so it is very important that parents collaborate effectively with teachers.

a1364.speaker: Representatives of the prefecture and the regional council
a1364.speech: Stressed that without mastery of this flagship discipline of basic school, which proves to be the key to all teaching of whatever nature, pupils' difficulties increase constantly; and urged parents to watch closely over their children's learning of reading during the first two years of their schooling.

a1466.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB)
a1466.speech: says Zambia, eSwatini, and Zimbabwe could see economic growth of six percent or more in 2025, backing a weak regional trend.

a1466.speaker: African Development Bank, African Economic Outlook 2025 (report)
a1466.speech: the bank noted that while Africa's overall growth prospects faced significant downside risks, a few countries were expected to maintain strong economic momentum ; "Despite the low regional growth outlook, a few countries – notably eSwatini, Zambia, and Zimbabwe – could achieve growth rates of six percent or higher in 2025," the report stated.

a1466.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB)
a1466.speech: The bank observed that the country's [South Africa's] ongoing efforts to address global trade disruptions and implement structural reforms could improve its medium-term growth trajectory.

a1466.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB)
a1466.speech: also cautioned that African countries could overturn the subdued growth outlook by mitigating the transmission of global shocks and economic uncertainty into domestic markets. However, this would hinge on several factors, including curbing inflation, addressing the continent's mounting debt, and the resilience of the global economy in the face of rising risks and fragile demand ; "Downside risks to the outlook include restricted trade, which could hamper growth directly by reducing business activity and indirectly through financial channels, weakening investor confidence and triggering capital outflows," it warned.

a1466.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB)
a1466.speech: the bank noted that persistent inflation, fuelled by entrenched domestic supply constraints and a diminished effectiveness of monetary policy in containing demand-driven price pressures, could dampen the expected growth rebound.

a1466.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB)
a1466.speech: the Bank highlighted risks to future [external financial] inflows due to aid cuts by key donors and heightened global uncertainty, although external financial inflows to Africa rebounded in 2023.

a1481.speaker: Dr Kalumbi Shangula, Minister of Health and Social Services of Namibia
a1481.speech: Said the boat is intended to deliver health services in the region, especially at times when the water is high. “The boat is worth about N$600,000. The boat was built to transport doctors, nurses and patients to health facilities, especially to places that are usually flooded, as well as to Impalila Island,” Shangula said. ; Shangula said that providing the boat demonstrates the ministry’s commitment to ensuring that every Namibian receives quality health care with dignity. ; “The situation of the Zambezi region makes it difficult for the ministry of health to treat citizens at certain times of the year because places become surrounded by flood water. This problem has been solved by the donation of this boat,” Shangula said. ; Shangula added that what is called the Universal Health Coverage Service Coverage Index currently stands at 63%. ; “Flooding does not only disrupt everyday life, it also obstructs health work. The boat will help children and women during difficult times, and also make it possible to respond to places where a particular disease has broken out,” Shangula said.

a1651.speaker: Merica Vilakati, Managing Director of Construction Associates
a1651.speech: presented a detailed progress report and confirmed that the project is progressing according to schedule and in line with the planned specifications.

a1651.speaker: Manqoba Khumalo, Minister of Commerce, Industry and Trade
a1651.speech: said the government welcomed the investment by Jonsson Workwear, highlighting its potential to drive job creation, industrial growth, and economic diversification ; "This project represents more than infrastructure; it reflects investor confidence in Eswatini and will create significant employment opportunities while boosting the country's manufacturing sector."

a1651.speaker: Prince Mcwasho, Head of Operations at Construction Associates
a1651.speech: reaffirmed Construction Associates' commitment to delivering the project to the highest standards and within the set timeframe.

a1651.speaker: Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade
a1651.speech: emphasised that investments such as the Jonsson Workwear facility align with the government's strategy to expand the industrial base, attract foreign direct investment, and strengthen Eswatini's competitiveness in the regional market.

a1894.speaker: Leelai M. Kpukuyou, former Secretary General of the Liberia Business Association (LIBA) (letter to President Joseph Nyuma Boakai)
a1894.speech: In her letter to the President, Kpukuyou extended her heartfelt congratulations on his leadership, stating, “Your guidance has given me and many others renewed hope for Liberia's future.” She emphasized her role as a proud ambassador for Liberia, noting, “For many people around the world, I may be the only Liberian they might interact with. I strive to represent our nation positively, encouraging investment and goodwill towards Liberia.”

a1894.speaker: Leelai M. Kpukuyou, former Secretary General of the Liberia Business Association (LIBA)
a1894.speech: On her qualifications: “My experience has equipped me with a unique understanding of the local business environment and the complexities of foreign direct investment,” she stated ; “My studies prepared me to effectively advocate for Liberia in international forums,” she noted.

a1894.speaker: Leelai M. Kpukuyou, former Secretary General of the Liberia Business Association (LIBA)
a1894.speech: Recalling a conversation with President Boakai during a visit to his home last November, Kpukuyou said, “You spoke passionately about your desire to see Liberia's economy thrive and improve the livelihood of ordinary Liberians.”

a1894.speaker: Leelai M. Kpukuyou, former Secretary General of the Liberia Business Association (LIBA)
a1894.speech: On her plans if appointed: “I believe Liberia is at a critical juncture, and the success of your administration depends on the collective efforts of all Liberians,” she asserted ; “I will invite business leaders—from small enterprises to large corporations—to work together and ensure the stability of essential commodities such as rice, petroleum, and cement.” ; “Strengthening these businesses is vital for improving Liberia's overall investment climate,” she emphasized ; “I am eager to contribute to your administration and our beloved country, Liberia,” she concluded in her letter to President Boakai. “Together, we can build a brighter economic future for all Liberians.”

a1916.speaker: Brian Siatubi, Konkola Copper Mines (KCM) Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) manager
a1916.speech: says the giant [...] (statement truncated in the article text) — on KCM allocating a US$1 million budget towards the Integrated Livelihood Project (ILP), including water reticulation, agriculture and livestock farming, for poverty alleviation and food security in communities where it operates.

a2140.speaker: Save the Children (NGO)
a2140.speech: Indicated that all children in the Gaza Strip face possible death from hunger or disease due to the impossibility of safely delivering humanitarian aid in the region since the Israeli military offensive in the enclave began ; stressed that the risk of famine will continue to increase as long as Israel keeps blocking the entry of aid, including food, water and hygiene products ; added that, between 1 January and 15 February, more than 50% of requests for humanitarian aid and assessment work in areas of northern Gaza were denied by the Israeli authorities.

a2140.speaker: Humanitarian worker for Save the Children in Rafah (unnamed)
a2140.speech: Reported that her relatives in the north of the Gaza Strip have adopted desperate measures to survive: "My husband told me that people are resorting to eating bird feed, animal feed and tree leaves out of desperation." ; "They have been forced to look for food scraps (everywhere). Recently, (the worker's husband) found food scraps at his sister's house that had already been bitten by rats, but he washed them and ate them anyway, because there was literally nothing else to eat. He says he will not die from the bombs, but from the lack of food."

a2140.speaker: Jason Lee, Save the Children Director in the Occupied Palestinian Territories
a2140.speech: Said that "there is mass starvation, of an entire people." ; "How can anyone live like this? After the immense number of deaths in this war, more than 28,000 people, 70% of them women and children, hunger is causing children and families to die in slow motion." ; said basic humanitarian aid has been provided in dribs and drabs or denied by the Israeli authorities, and basic services have been reduced by the continuous fighting, stating that "the conditions for providing humanitarian aid to the children of Gaza are not being met, and are also getting worse." ; argued that "the only way to end this, to keep children and families alive, is an immediate and definitive ceasefire and an immediate increase in unrestricted humanitarian aid", warning that "without all of this, a meaningful response in Gaza is impossible and children will continue to die."

a2140.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a2140.speech: Announced on Tuesday a pause in the delivery of food aid in the north of the Gaza Strip, citing security reasons, just two days after the UN agency resumed operations ; claimed that its convoys were attacked by "groups of hungry people," including attempts by those people to board the trucks, and stated that another of the deliveries "faced total chaos and violence due to the collapse of civil order."

a2140.speaker: WFP, World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF (joint warning)
a2140.speech: Warned on Monday that acute malnutrition among children and pregnant and breastfeeding women in Gaza is increasing sharply - with an especially serious situation in the north - which is about to cause an "explosion of deaths" in the Palestinian enclave.

a2169.speaker: Mohamed Abdallah Mahyoub, Secretary General of MENFOP (Djibouti Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training)
a2169.speech: Urged the participants, and in particular the representatives of the major local hotels and the French Forces in Djibouti (FFDj), to share with the technicians all their remarks and reflections on the document presented.

a2216.speaker: Civil libertarians
a2216.speech: Said people who take part in Saturday's mass "No Kings" protest against President Donald Trump's administration may be targeted for federal government surveillance with a range of technology that could include facial recognition and phone hacking.

a2216.speaker: Thorin Klosowski, security and privacy activist with the Electronic Frontier Foundation
a2216.speech: Said Friday that the level of surveillance at protests and the type of technology in use is likely to be both location-specific and dependent on the police forces present.

a2216.speaker: Thorin Klosowski, security and privacy activist with the Electronic Frontier Foundation
a2216.speech: "Even just what lawmakers are saying is very different this time around. I'm a little more worried this time than I was last time."

a2216.speaker: Ryan Shapiro, executive director of government transparency group Property of the People
a2216.speech: Said in an email Friday: "Under previous administrations, law enforcement surveillance of peaceful demonstrations was already commonplace and corrosive of free expression" ; "Given Trump's open hostility to even minor dissent, such surveillance now poses an existential threat to what remains of American democracy and only underscores the need for mass protest."

a2216.speaker: Brennan Center
a2216.speech: According to the Brennan Center, multiple federal agencies have deployed social media monitoring.

a2216.speaker: Department of Homeland Security
a2216.speech: Department of Homeland Security officials didn't directly respond to a query about potential surveillance of "No Kings" protesters; "As it does every day, DHS law enforcement will enforce the laws of our nation," the department said in a statement.

a2216.speaker: ICE spokesperson
a2216.speech: Told Reuters in an email Saturday that "the First Amendment protects speech and peaceful assembly — not rioting. DHS is taking reasonable and constitutional measures to uphold the rule of law and protect our officers."

a2216.speaker: Stateline (news outlet)
a2216.speech: Reported in February that multiple local police departments have used facial recognition technology, with laws governing its use varying from state to state.

a2216.speaker: Nate Wessler, deputy director of the ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project
a2216.speech: Said that different technologies have different legal requirements and require specific court authorization for focused and limited use, but that it's not easy to prove that a specific person was included in an inappropriate collection of data ; "This is a recurring problem in trying to constrain government's use of surveillance technologies. They are often designed to work surreptitiously and it can be extremely hard to prove whether you or any particular person was swept up in this kind of surveillance."

a2216.speaker: Nate Wessler, deputy director of the ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project
a2216.speech: Said drones collecting footage raise concerns about government chilling of First Amendment rights: "If you have a group of overwhelmingly peaceful protesters with a permit in the streets doing their thing, there's no good reason why you should have a drone watching everything they do."

a2216.speaker: Don Bell, policy counsel for the Constitution Project at the Project on Government Oversight
a2216.speech: Said the Trump administration "sidelined or fired" Homeland Security staffers who might have curbed surveillance "excesses" ; "One of the reasons why the use of these technologies is uniquely dangerous is that there are virtually no legal guardrails in place to prevent mass surveillance, and what did exist has been bulldozed."

a2216.speaker: Donald Trump and his allies
a2216.speech: Have increasingly criticized the follow-up event and described the protesters as terrorists, Hamas supporters and far-left agitators, without presenting any evidence.

a2216.speaker: Democratic senators
a2216.speech: In July asked Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem detailed questions about surveillance technology used to monitor protests.

a2216.speaker: Office of Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey
a2216.speech: Said the agency never responded to the senators' questions about surveillance technology.

a2216.speaker: Ed Markey, Massachusetts Senator
a2216.speech: Said in an email: "Donald Trump has shown he'll aggressively weaponize government powers to squelch dissent. At this weekend's 'No Kings' protests, the Trump administration must refrain from surveilling Americans who are exercising their constitutional rights."

a2216.speaker: Central California Intelligence Center (fusion center alert document obtained by Property of the People)
a2216.speech: The document identified Sacramento, Fresno, and Stockton among dozens of "No Kings" protest sites and, noting that while the protests were billed as "nonviolent action," the center said additional intelligence reports were being planned on the rallies; the center did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

a2216.speaker: National Fusion Center Association
a2216.speech: Did not directly address questions about October 18 plans, but referred Reuters to a 2011 federal document listing recommendations for law enforcement agencies regarding "First Amendment-Protected Events."

a2219.speaker: Harouna Kaboré, Minister in charge of Trade
a2219.speech: Expressed the wish that Burkina Faso be among the biggest honey-producing countries on the African continent, alongside Ethiopia, Tanzania, Kenya and the Central African Republic, and noted a "clear improvement" in beekeeping activity in the "Land of Upright People" ; "In Burkina Faso, beekeeping is a fast-growing sector to which the government is giving all the attention it requires. Over the period 2011-2015, average annual honey production was estimated at 500 tonnes with average annual income of 1.5 billion FCFA. These figures rose to 1,000 tonnes in 2018 for income of more than 2.6 billion FCFA, generated and distributed among nearly 16,300 actors working individually or in associations in the sector."

a2219.speaker: Sommanogo Koutou, Minister in charge of Animal Resources
a2219.speech: Added that beyond these products, bees play an important role in the pollination of plants, at around 70%, and thus contribute to the preservation of biodiversity and to food security.

a2219.speaker: Désiré Yaméogo, representative of the Interprofessionnel miel (honey interprofessional body)
a2219.speech: Said that with this 1st edition of SANAM a "new page" is opening for beekeeping in Burkina Faso.

a2219.speaker: Sékou Oumar Doudou Doumbia, Vice-President of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Burkina Faso (CCI-BF)
a2219.speech: Said the National Honey Fair is intended as a framework for promoting national honey and derived products ; "SANAM aims to create a framework for exchanges and business meetings for professionals in the sector. For this 1st edition, planned events include an inaugural conference on the central theme, a master class on putting the best beekeeping methods and tools into practice, B2B meetings and an exhibition-sale."

a2219.speaker: Sékou Oumar Doudou Doumbia, Vice-President of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Burkina Faso (CCI-BF)
a2219.speech: Reaffirmed, on behalf of his hierarchy, the Chamber of Commerce's commitment to working in synergy with the other partner actors to achieve the objectives set.

a2296.speaker: Romeo Muyunda, spokesperson of the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism (Namibia)
a2296.speech: has confirmed the water situation at Ngenda; Muyunda stated that samples were taken from the water treatment plant in 2023 for testing, and it was determined that the water posed a low health risk.

a2296.speaker: Pohamba Shifeta, Minister of Environment, Forestry and Tourism (Namibia)
a2296.speech: has urged the tourism industry and reservation services to up their service delivery to grow the industry. Shifeta said this during the opening of the 2024 Namibia Tourism Expo.

a2296.speaker: Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism (Namibia)
a2296.speech: says Germany's decision to restrict or ban the import of hunting trophies could harm Namibia's conservation efforts.

a2296.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a2296.speech: has commended the Namibian Exile Kids Association (NEKA) for continuing to be the voice of the children born in exile at the height of the liberation struggle.

a2332.speaker: Ministry of Environment, Forestry, and Tourism (MEFT)
a2332.speech: Announced that it granted approval for the export of 42 live white rhinoceroses to the United States, noting the rhinos are privately owned and not government property, as only black rhinos are state-owned in Namibia.

a2332.speaker: Government of Namibia
a2332.speech: Has maintained its stance on the export of minerals in their raw forms.

a2332.speaker: Ministry of Agriculture, Water, and Land Reform (MAWLR)
a2332.speech: Announced that Namibian beef and lamb can now be exported to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Qatar.

a2332.speaker: Lucia Iipumbu, Minister of Trade
a2332.speech: Disclosed that Namibia's exports to Japan are notably lower than its imports, with exports amounting to N$90 million while imports reached N$1.4 billion.

a2332.speaker: MeatCo
a2332.speech: Says it has introduced a number of reforms and restructuring to remain afloat, despite natural calamities which affected the livestock sector.

a2332.speaker: Maxwell Nghidinwa, farm Manager at Sikondo Green Scheme, Kavango West Region
a2332.speech: Is of the view that Namibia's green schemes can be more competitive if the country finds export markets.

a2619.speaker: Elijah Ngurare, Prime Minister of Namibia
a2619.speech: Said the situation of Angolan kids as young as four years old on the streets is a case the government regards as urgent.

a2619.speaker: Lucia Witbooi, Vice President of Namibia
a2619.speech: Called on Lüderitz councillors and community members to collectively address challenges facing the local disability centre during her visit.

a2619.speaker: Suzan Ndjaleka, deputy minister of health and social services
a2619.speech: Has called for teamwork and unity from the health staff to improve Namibians’ access to health care and social services.

a2619.speaker: MPs (Namibian National Assembly)
a2619.speech: Raised various concerns regarding the budget allocation towards the Ministry of Health and Social Services and gave their suggestions on where they expect to see improvement in the sector and how it could be better capacitated to cater to all citizens nationwide.

a2619.speaker: Ministry of Health and Social Services (Namibia)
a2619.speech: Has reaffirmed that it is making rehabilitation and assistive technology services available across the country; currently such services are offered free of charge only at seven hospitals.

a2619.speaker: Kalumbi Shangula, Health and Social Services Minister
a2619.speech: Says the ability to see and the gift of vision are two of the most essential aspects of human health and well-being.

a2619.speaker: Kalumbi Shangula, Minister of Health and Social Services
a2619.speech: Has responded to concerns raised by Popular Democratic Movement (PDM) MP Winnie Moongo about the shortage of cardiotocography papers at Windhoek Central Hospital.

a2619.speaker: Winnie Moongo, Popular Democratic Movement (PDM) MP
a2619.speech: Raised concerns about the shortage of cardiotocography papers at Windhoek Central Hospital.

a2740.speaker: U.S. Ambassador to Mozambique
a2740.speech: Warns that the withdrawal of USAID staff from the country could result in “great vulnerability”; states in an urgent cable to the Secretary of State that the complete withdrawal of USAID staff would be a high-risk measure that would make it impossible for the U.S. government to properly manage $1.5 billion in aid programmes, a large part of which goes to life-saving humanitarian assistance ; said that the absence of experienced agency staff in Mozambique would leave 114 ongoing funding initiatives and more than 225 junior workers in a state of uncertainty.

a2740.speaker: The New York Times (newspaper report)
a2740.speech: Reported that other diplomats across the continent are sending similar cables to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in an attempt to preserve programmes on which millions of Africans depend; obtained a copy of the ambassador's urgent cable.

a2800.speaker: Puntland State of Somalia (government appeal)
a2800.speech: has made an urgent appeal for humanitarian and stabilization assistance for residents affected by ongoing military operations targeting Islamic State (ISIS) militants in the remote mountains of the Bari region.

a2800.speaker: Puntland government reports
a2800.speech: According to government reports, over 19,640 families have been uprooted by the counter-terrorism operation, which was launched in late December under the codename "Operation Hillaac."

a2800.speaker: Abdi Farah Said, Puntland Interior Minister
a2800.speech: called on United Nations agencies and other international partners to provide immediate assistance to displaced families and communities affected by the conflict: "We are particularly appealing to UN agencies to provide humanitarian aid to those affected by the ongoing operation. Additionally, we urge agencies involved in stabilization projects, such as USAID, to assist communities in the liberated areas." ; emphasized the need for essential services in the areas cleared of militants, including education, healthcare, water, and roads: "These services will enable displaced locals to resume their livelihoods and allow the government to ensure their safety once they return."

a2800.speaker: Ubah Abdirashid Mohamed Hirsi, Puntland's Minister of Humanitarian Management
a2800.speech: confirmed the staggering displacement numbers: "So far, 19,640 families have fled their homes and are in desperate need of emergency support. Poor rainfall last year compounded the difficulties these families were already facing, and now this displacement has worsened their situation."

a2800.speaker: Mohamud Aideed Dirir, Puntland Minister of Information
