a2800.speech: praised the progress made by Puntland Security Forces (PSF), despite limited resources: "The counter-ISIS operation, which we initially projected to take months, has achieved remarkable success in just a few weeks. ISIS fighters are on the run, abandoning their positions, and Puntland forces are pursuing them in the remote mountains." ; commended local communities for their role in providing intelligence that has been instrumental in tracking the militants.

a3071.speaker: Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, Minister of National Education and Vocational Training (MENFOP) of Djibouti
a3071.speech: Spoke to stress the value of reading and writing for children who acquire a taste for them from the earliest age — the essential message of the event, addressed also to parents, who must help create a love of reading in children; he highlighted the main moments and flagship activities planned throughout the reading week, which will be run in twenty-seven schools across the country by about ten writers and authors eager to share their tastes and their passion for books with pupils.

a3071.speaker: Lloyd Jackson, USAID representative
a3071.speech: Said he was happy to take part in the workshops with enthusiastic pupils, and reaffirmed his organisation’s support for MENFOP’s work to strengthen the quality of teaching and learning.

a3082.speaker: Heads of foreign missions in Liberia (Diplomatic Corps)
a3082.speech: Promise to support the Government of Liberia in the wake of the United States’ cut in aid; the Diplomatic Corps, including Ambassadors from Cameroon, Nigeria, the EU, Germany, the UK, and UN Women, reaffirmed their support for Liberia during this difficult time, asserting that their countries will stand with Liberia in thick and thin, despite ongoing challenges engulfing the country due to the indefinite suspension of all USAID-funded projects.

a3082.speaker: Dephue Zuo, Liberia’s Deputy Minister for Economic Management
Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberia’s Finance Minister
a3082.speech: Emphasized the need for continued partnership with international donors; expressed confidence that Liberia will overcome this challenge, citing past crises like the 2008/2009 global food, fuel, and financial crisis, the Ebola outbreak, and the COVID-19 pandemic; stressed that strong support from Liberia’s bilateral and multilateral partners is key to enabling the country to address those crises.

a3082.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberia’s Finance Minister
a3082.speech: Notes that expenditure rationalization and robust domestic resource mobilization are the key measures the government is implementing to address the crises; informed partners that, as the situation evolves, the government will take further proactive and reactive measures to mitigate the shock’s impact; states that the government will be intervening to continue some critical interventions in health and education that the USAID aid cut will affect and calls on scale-up support from other partners to assist or complement the government’s response.

a3082.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberia’s Finance Minister
a3082.speech: Tells Ambassadors at the meeting that the government will provide further updates to partners in coming weeks and that government, with support from the UN Resident Coordinator’s Office and UNDP, is planning a Partners Roundtable at end of March 2025 to further discuss the USAID aid and support to the ARREST AGENDA for Inclusive Development (AAID).

a3082.speaker: European Union Ambassador to Liberia
a3082.speech: Announced that the EU would support Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) in observing the Nimba By-election.

a3183.speaker: Stakeholders in Taraba State and beyond
a3183.speech: Submit she has lived up to the expectations of her Principal, the Governor of Taraba State, Dr. Agbu Kefas, within a short time ; Have described the amazons as "Possible Solution" to the state's education challenges.

a3183.speaker: Rabi Sunday, Acting Chairman of the Taraba State Universal Basic Education Board (SUBEB)
a3183.speech: Said in an interview with Daily Independent that the Taraba State government has demonstrated avowed commitment and provision of resources in addressing identifiable gaps in the sector regarded as the gateway to development ; Speaking of measures to actualise the free quality and compulsory education policy of the Taraba State government: "Our students enrollment has increased beyond our imaginations. Indeed, the decision of Governor on education has addressed school dropouts challenge and has also addressed youth restiveness."

a3183.speaker: Benjamin Tanko, a teacher in Wukari Local Government Education Authority
a3183.speech: Said in an interview with Daily Independent that Rabi has the experience and understood the nitty-gritty of the Board, saying she has brought her clear understanding to bear in the discharge of her responsibility and capacity as the Acting Chairman.

a3183.speaker: Rabi Sunday, Acting Chairman of the Taraba State Universal Basic Education Board (SUBEB)
a3183.speech: Reiterated the commitment of the Taraba State government to the development and positive outcomes of education in the state: "We remain grateful to the government of Dr. Agbu Kefas, for keeping to his campaign promise. I remembered during his campaign, he gave the people of the state his words on education and I am happy that he has fulfilled his promise. There is an increment in school enrollment and there is a reduction in the Out-of-School-Children. His policy of free and compulsory education has addressed some of the challenges facing basic education in the state. This has endeared him to the people of the state as education is developing in Taraba State."

a3274.speaker: Patrick Nakolendousse, President of the Federation of Associations of United Nations System Staff
a3274.speech: Underlined the motivation behind the gesture: "In this spirit of solidarity, we launched a voluntary fundraising initiative among the staff of the United Nations system, in order to support the most vulnerable people in Burkina Faso. Thanks to this collective momentum, we were able to gather the sum of 6,460,580 CFA francs intended for the National Solidarity Fund, in support of the authorities' efforts."

a3274.speaker: Representative of the Resident Coordinator of the United Nations system in Burkina Faso
a3274.speech: Warmly welcomed the initiative, describing it as the very embodiment of the organisation's values: "This gesture demonstrates, once again, that our role goes beyond that of mere workers. We are above all bearers of the fundamental values of the organisation: solidarity, dignity and assistance to the most vulnerable." ; stressed that the action marks the beginning of a lasting commitment: "This is only a beginning. We will remain mobilised and we will continue to invest ourselves, voluntarily, to come to the aid of populations in distress."

a3274.speaker: Dr Sami Nicolas Kambou, Director General of the National Fund for Solidarity and Social Resilience
a3274.speech: Warmly welcomed the donation and, representing the Secretary General of the ministry, underlined the impact of the contribution: "This surge of solidarity allows us to bring more support to vulnerable people. It will also contribute to the empowerment of some of them, so that they become genuine economic actors in the service of the development of Burkina Faso."

a3274.speaker: The donors (United Nations system staff)
a3274.speech: Said the initiative aims to support the most vulnerable populations of Burkina Faso, in the face of the security crisis the country is going through.

a3293.speaker: Elon Musk (post on X)
a3293.speech: Had accused the country of imposing “openly racist property laws”, in reference to Black Economic Empowerment (BEE), which requires foreign companies to cede 30% of their capital to historically disadvantaged groups.

a3293.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3293.speech: On Sunday, threatened to suspend American aid to South Africa, accusing Pretoria of confiscating land and discriminating against certain populations.

a3293.speaker: South African Presidency
a3293.speech: Confirmed the conversation with Musk, specifying that Ramaphosa reaffirmed the values of equality, justice and respect for the rule of law enshrined in the Constitution. He also denied Trump’s accusations, asserting that land reform aims at a more equitable redistribution of land and that no confiscation has taken place.

a3293.speaker: Africanews (source)
a3293.speech: Cited as the source of the report.

a3394.speaker: Han Kang, acting USAID deputy assistant administrator for global health and director of the USAID office of HIV and Aids
a3394.speech: Revealed this week that South Africa remains a key territory for US-funded HIV and Aids work as the focus increasingly shifts to the search for viable vaccines ; "We [last week] launched a new research and development activity, where we are directly funding African-based scientists to do vaccine research and development, in particular in South Africa with the Medical Research Council," said Kang.

a3394.speaker: PEPFAR (@PEPFAR, social media post, September 19, 2023)
a3394.speech: "HIV/AIDS infections and deaths plummeted, in no small part because of #PEPFAR's work in more than 55 countries, saving more than 25 million lives." Thank you @POTUS for sharing why you are #ProudofPEPFAR at #UNGA78.

a3394.speaker: Dr Ernest Darkoh, co-founder of BroadReach
a3394.speech: "One of our greatest joint achievements was turning around the Ugu District in KwaZulu-Natal, which at one point had the highest HIV prevalence in the world. Millions of lives were saved by our health workers, whose capacity was extended with the help of artificial intelligence," he said.

a3394.speaker: Dhirisha Naidoo, PEPFAR-funded programme worker in the Ugu District under BroadReach
a3394.speech: Said that once ARTs became available and the support structure was in place, Ugu's turnaround was remarkable ; "Ugu became the first district in SA to reach the 90-90-90 UNAID care and treatment goals. We are proud that, just last week, two more of our districts also reached this milestone! We currently support 555 000 people on sustained treatment across four rural, high-prevalence districts in KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga," she said.

a3394.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a3394.speech: According to the WHO, around 7.5 million people were living with HIV in South Africa; and PEPFAR has been a spectacular success in battling the pandemic in Africa, a continent more severely hit by HIV, with an estimated 30 million fatalities since 1982 - adult infection rates in Africa were 6.1% in late 2005, compared to 1% globally, but by 2007 they had decreased to 5%, as opposed to 8% globally.

a3394.speaker: Chris Collins, president and CEO of Friends of the Global Fight Against AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria
a3394.speech: "It is unfair that people die around the world because of a lack of access to lifesaving drugs. For the global community to reach its goal of ending HIV as a public health crisis by 2030, we must continue to advocate for universal access to healthcare and the achievement of greater diversity, equity and inclusion in global healthcare. This will be possible if PEPFAR is reauthorised and given the green light to scale its innovations and networks to reach more people," said Collins.

a3509.speaker: Mozambican state budget proposal (PESOE 2026), obtained by Lusa
a3509.speech: The Mozambican government forecasts economic growth of 3.2% in 2026, which would raise the country's gross domestic product to 1.665 trillion meticais (€22.3 billion); it projects a nominal GDP of 1.544 trillion meticais for 2025, annual inflation moderating to 3.7% in 2026, net international reserves covering 4.4 months of imports, public expenditure at around 32% of GDP, revenues at 28% of GDP and a fiscal deficit of about 6% of GDP.

a3509.speaker: Amílcar Tivane, Secretary of State for Treasury and Budget
a3509.speech: “The objective is to consolidate public accounts, stabilise debt indicators and maintain space for productive investment,” additionally noting that global shocks and geopolitical factors continue to affect Mozambique's projections ; said the government would continue to prioritise fiscal credibility and transparency while implementing reforms to strengthen revenue collection.

a3547.speaker: Hayden Dahmm, TReNDS Manager, and Tom Moultrie, Professor of Demography at UCT (authors)
a3547.speech: Write that “we must be wary of ‘data colonialism’ – the potential for the powerful, data-rich countries and corporations in the Global North to undercut capacity development in the Global South by failing to recognise the local context”, and encourage further consideration and discussion of this issue within the global statistical community as it gathers for the UN Statistical Commission.

a3547.speaker: Hayden Dahmm, TReNDS Manager, and Tom Moultrie, Professor of Demography at UCT (authors)
a3547.speech: Argue that increased dependency on the Global North for technical infrastructure, science and data-based solutions risks crowding out Southern countries’ own data needs, since donors are significant external funders of NSOs and this relationship “can create incentives that channel resources away from domestic needs in favour of donor data requirements”, a dynamic that “parallels how colonial systems were administrated for the primary benefit of Western powers”; and warn that over-reliance on emerging technologies produced in the Global North could leave marginalised areas under-served or completely overlooked.

a3547.speaker: Hayden Dahmm, TReNDS Manager, and Tom Moultrie, Professor of Demography at UCT (authors)
a3547.speech: Recommend several actions to support NSOs – mapping data gaps or needs in close work with governments; adequately funding NSOs in low-income countries with greater donor coordination so that statistical systems can prioritise the data needs of domestic policymakers; ensuring NSO officials and local academics are actively involved in managing new data sources with fully transparent methodologies; commitments by international organisations to build sustainability in local data production; clear guidance and standards for public-private data collaborations; and having extra-national data complement rather than supplant domestic data – plus wider government measures including data-driven government strategies with good digital governance, effective tech-sector regulation, “localising” data and examining opportunities around “nationalising” data, concluding that “the ‘data revolution’ will only be revolutionary if it genuinely empowers those who currently lack power.”

a3547.speaker: Recent surveys of national statistical offices (NSOs)
a3547.speech: Found that nine out of 10 NSOs in low and lower-middle-income countries may not fully be able to meet their international reporting requirements.

a3547.speaker: Nick Couldry and Ulises Mejias, authors of “The Costs of Connection”
a3547.speech: Posit that the emerging state of data-driven capitalism is a continuation of the systems of exploitation that defined previous colonial eras; paralleling past patterns of colonial resource extraction, many Northern corporations profit from the personal data they are gathering around the world and are undermining the data sovereignty of nations in the Global South.

a3547.speaker: 2018 survey of NSO representatives from 140 low and middle-income countries
a3547.speech: Found that respondents ranked international development partners as the most important users of official statistics, well above government ministries, local government and civil society.

a3547.speaker: OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC)
a3547.speech: Has noted insufficient donor alignment with national priorities as a major bottleneck for statistical systems, as conflicting demands from donors for particular datasets can further erode domestic demand for data and entrench dependence on donors; has also called for greater coordination of donor funding at the country level.

a3547.speaker: Accuracy test of electrification rates calculated from Linescan night-time light data in Burkina Faso
a3547.speech: Found that up to 57% of the 147 communities sampled were undetectable.

a3547.speaker: MIT Technology Review (recent article)
a3547.speech: Described how global AI groups often lack geographical diversity, creating the risk of AI standards that will perpetuate biases and fail to account for cultural contexts.

a3564.speaker: Dr Doto Biteko, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Energy of Tanzania
a3564.speech: Took centre stage at the launch, underscoring the importance of investing heavily in education; reminded everyone that education is the ultimate gift – you can lose your possessions, but no one can ever snatch away your learning; argued that quality education is the key to navigating this storm of change and coming out stronger; emphasised that education can’t be left to the Ministry of Education alone, but requires a multisectoral team effort, and that collaboration is key to creating leaders who can confidently steer Tanzania’s development agenda.

a3564.speaker: Simon Nanyaro, Board Chairperson of the Tanzania Education Network (TEN/MET)
a3564.speech: Highlighted that this year’s conference couldn’t have come at a better time, calling it a platform to rethink and reinforce education systems through locally driven investments – helping reduce dependence on foreign aid, increase equity and boost accountability; lauded the Tanzanian government’s efforts, especially policy reforms, curriculum updates, new infrastructure and teacher recruitment that demonstrate real commitment to decongest classrooms and enhance learning environments.

a3564.speaker: Martha Makala, National Coordinator (TEN/MET)
a3564.speech: Echoed this optimism, underscoring the importance of turning conference discussions into practical action – the goal is to come out with workable plans that will tangibly improve education across Tanzania and the wider African continent; thanked the Ministry of Education and funding partners like the Mastercard Foundation and Global Partnership for Education for making the event a success.

a3592.speaker: Spokesman for British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak
a3592.speech: sent out to decry the dismissal of English batsman Jonny Bairstow: "The prime minister agrees with (England captain) Ben Stokes who said he simply wouldn't want to win a game in the manner that Australia did."

a3592.speaker: Ben Stokes, England cricket captain
a3592.speech: said he simply wouldn't want to win a game in the manner that Australia did.

a3592.speaker: Anthony Albanese, Australian Prime Minister
a3592.speech: shot back that he was "proud" of Australia's "men's and women's cricket teams, who have both won their opening two Ashes matches against England." "Same old Aussies - always winning!" he added. "(I) look forward to welcoming them home victorious."

a3592.speaker: Spokesman for British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak
a3592.speech: said Sunak did deplore abuse directed at the Australians by Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) members: "He thinks it was right that the MCC have taken swift action to suspend any members accused of poor behaviour" ; remarked that while there is a "friendly rivalry" over sport between the two leaders, Sunak does not view cricket as a core diplomatic issue; "The game did provide an opportunity to see Ben Stokes at his best and it was an incredible Test match -- he has confidence that England will bounce back."

a3592.speaker: Brendon McCullum, England cricket coach
a3592.speech: believes the incident can act as a lightning rod for a fightback in the series: "In the end, they made a play, they've got to live with that. We would have made a different play but that's life. In time, we'll see, but I get the feeling that it might have an effect on them. I don't know if it's anger, but our unit is galvanised. There are times as a coach where you've got to reduce emotion because it's going to bubble over and you can make poor decisions, but there's times when you allow emotion to go because it's going to galvanise the unit. That's what I felt this emotion did for the side. I looked around the group and the guys were a little upset. If that helps us to win those key moments in the next Test, then I'm all for it."

a3592.speaker: Geoffrey Boycott, former England captain (writing in the Daily Telegraph)
a3592.speech: has called for Australia to apologise: "Australia need to have a think about what they did and make a full public apology. We all make mistakes in the heat of the moment. People will think better of the Australians if they put their hands up and say "we got it wrong". That is the way to go. Let's see over the next few days if they are man enough to do that."

a3621.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe
a3621.speech: Made a renewed call for African unity, economic freedom, and justice for people of African descent, hailing Africa Day as a moment of reflection, celebration, and renewed commitment to the continent’s founding ideals: “Sixty-two years ago, African nations stood at the crossroads of history, emerging from the shadows of colonial rule and seeking to define the shared destiny of the peoples of this great Continent. The establishment of the OAU was undoubtedly a bold declaration that Africa was no longer willing to be divided by oppressive racist regimes.” He said the country paid tribute to the sacrifices of liberation heroes across the continent, highlighting the pivotal role of the OAU’s Liberation Committee in supporting the country’s struggle for independence.

a3621.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe
a3621.speech: Reaffirmed his commitment to the AU’s Agenda 2063 and regional economic integration through initiatives like the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), and vowed to harness the country’s natural resources and home-grown solutions for sustainable development: “Unity is our greatest strength. The emphatic calls made those decades ago, with regards to the importance of solidarity among African nations; ‘African solutions to African problems’ and the importance of Africa’s natural resources to benefit her peoples, must echo louder in our present time. The freedom we enjoy today across our motherland, and mother Continent of Africa was not handed over on a silver platter. It was the result of unparalleled sacrifice of the gallant sons and daughters of the soil, many of whom paid with their lives.”

a3621.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe
a3621.speech: Called for a more inclusive and representative global political and financial system: “Africa’s voice must be heard,” he declared, particularly on matters such as climate change, debt, and economic inequality, adding that the current international system must be reformed to reflect the realities and needs of African nations. He pledged continued cooperation within the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and with the African Diaspora, acknowledging the vital role of Africans abroad in the continent’s development.

a3621.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe
a3621.speech: In a warning against the threat of neo-colonialism, made a rallying cry: “Never again should our continent be under foreign subjugation. The unity, peace, and prosperity of Africa depend on all of us—both on the continent and in the Diaspora.”

a3629.speaker: All project directors of MCA-Benin (in the documentary)
a3629.speech: Spoke to shed light on what the programme has already done, what it intends to do in the future, and what the population can hope for once all the works are completed.

a3706.speaker: Oumar Sogoba, Secretary General of the Ministry of Security and Civil Protection of Mali
a3706.speech: Said that the centre is a four-storey building that cost more than 1 billion FCFA.

a3706.speaker: Colonel Cheick Fanta Mady Koné, coordinator of HYDROMET-Mali
a3706.speech: Indicated that the CNOU will allow better coordination of interventions, more effective management of emergencies and a significant reduction in the loss of human life, property and the environment.

a3730.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3730.speech: Mentioned Lesotho in his address to US Congress while listing some of the foreign spending he had cut as “appalling waste” ; “Eight million dollars to promote LGBTQI+ in the African nation of Lesotho, which nobody has ever heard of.”

a3730.speaker: Lejone Mpotjoane, Lesotho's Foreign Minister
a3730.speech: Said on Wednesday he was shocked and insulted by US President Donald Trump saying nobody has heard of the African country, and invited him to come visit ; said the remark was “quite insulting” ; “I’m really shocked that my country can be referred to like that by the head of state” ; “Lesotho is such a significant and unique country in the whole world. I would be happy to invite the president, as well as the rest of the world to come to Lesotho” ; “The decision by the president to cut the aid… it is (his) prerogative to do that. We have to accept that. But to refer to my country like that, it is quite unfortunate.”

a3730.speaker: Lejone Mpotjoane, Lesotho's Foreign Minister
a3730.speech: Said some civil society organizations funded by the US Embassy in Lesotho did work to support the LGBT+ community, but the United States also provided important funding for the country’s health and agriculture sectors ; said Lesotho was feeling the impact as the health sector had been reliant on that aid for some time, but that the government was looking at how to become more self-sufficient.

a3950.speaker: Ousman Surur, Director of the Federal Cooperative Agency (Ethiopia)
a3950.speech: “The blending factories are meant to increase the production and productivity of the farmers in the country through the supply of appropriate fertilizer to the soils” ; on the failure after the Ministry of Agriculture and ATA purchased non-essential fertilizers of Boron, Zinc and potash amounting to 271,680 quintals: “The blending factory quit producing as the result of unspecified fertilizers purchased as an input.”

a3950.speaker: Agricultural Transformation Agency (ATA) 2013/14 report
a3950.speech: Indicated that sulfur, potassium, boron and zinc nutrients are deficient in many areas, so that one compound fertilizer NPS and five blended fertilizers – NPSB, NPKSB, NPSZnB, NPKSZnB, and NPSZn – are needed to address the key nutrient deficiencies in the tested soils.

a3950.speaker: Federal Cooperative Agency (Ethiopia)
a3950.speech: According to the agency, Gibe Dedessa and Becho Weliso Farmers’ Cooperative Union in Oromia Regional state registered success at least in small scale for the first batch of production ; the government is to pay nearly 252.7 million birr to the cooperatives based on the report of the Auditor General.

a4279.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4279.speech: Said Gaza is the "hungriest place on Earth" and the enclave's entire 2.3 million people face "catastrophic hunger".

a4279.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4279.speech: Said a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas is "very close", and could be announced as early as today.

a4279.speaker: Gaza's Health Ministry
a4279.speech: According to it, Israel's war on Gaza has killed at least 54,321 Palestinians and wounded 123,770.

a4279.speaker: Government Media Office (Gaza)
a4279.speech: Updated its death toll to more than 61,700, saying thousands of people missing under the rubble are presumed dead.

a4311.speaker: Human Sciences Research Council (think tank)
a4311.speech: Released figures in 2024 showing that Majola’s province recorded the second-highest HIV prevalence in the country, at 16%, with at least 1,300 young people estimated to contract the disease every week; the think tank says the district of Umgungundlovu has the highest number of HIV cases in South Africa.

a4311.speaker: South African health ministry
a4311.speech: According to the health ministry, PEPFAR contributes more than $400 million a year to South Africa’s HIV programmes and nongovernmental organisations, about 17% of the total funding.

a4311.speaker: UN Aids agency
a4311.speech: According to the UN Aids agency, PEPFAR is credited with saving at least 26 million lives globally since its inception in 2003.

a4311.speaker: US federal judge (court order)
a4311.speech: Ordered the Trump administration last week to temporarily lift the funding freeze.

a4311.speaker: US embassy in South Africa
a4311.speech: Said PEPFAR projects would resume under a limited waiver.

a4311.speaker: Majola, HIV patient in the Umzimkhulu region
a4311.speech: “Things will be tough around here, and a lot of people will default on their treatment because we really struggle with transport. The mobile clinics hardly come here.”

a4311.speaker: Manager at a health clinic in Umgungundlovu (anonymous, not authorised to speak to the press)
a4311.speech: “People who were doing administration and data capturing, whose salaries were funded by PEPFAR, have left. We are a small facility and we cannot handle such a workload.”

a4311.speaker: Nozuko Ngcaweni, HIV patient on treatment for about 30 years
a4311.speech: Said the aid suspension already impacted her community and many missed their treatment: “Not long ago, we said by 2030, we want to see an HIV-free generation. But if things remain as is, we will not achieve that. We will have to deal with deaths.”

a4311.speaker: Mzamo Zondi, provincial manager of the Treatment Action Campaign
a4311.speech: “Our response (to HIV) is likely to falter as we struggle to stop newly infected cases. This is a matter of life and death.”

a4316.speaker: Binyerem Ukaire, Director of Family Health, Federal Ministry of Health
a4316.speech: In response to enquiries, Ms Ukaire simply said, “To get reaction from the government, you need to go through the right channel.” (Repeated efforts to get a response from the health ministry on the reason for the cut were unsuccessful.)

a4316.speaker: United Nations (report, Trends in Maternal Mortality)
a4316.speech: Recently warned that global reductions in health aid could reverse decades of progress in tackling maternal mortality; the report attributed the 40 per cent global decline in maternal deaths between 2000 and 2023 to improved access to critical health services, and found Nigeria had the highest estimated number of maternal deaths in 2020, more than one-quarter (28.5 per cent) of the global total, with approximately 82,000 maternal deaths.

a4316.speaker: Stanley Ukpai, Director of Programmes, development Research and Projects Centre (dRPC)
a4316.speech: Expressed concerns with the reduction, saying Nigeria is still struggling to close a longstanding gap in family planning funding and has depended heavily on external sources for years: “In 2024, we saw a significant step forward with the N2.2 billion allocation, which was an attempt to address the financing gap. I understand that the funds were eventually released in December,” ; “But we were shocked to see that only N66 million was allocated for family planning in 2025.”

a4316.speaker: Stanley Ukpai, Director of Programmes, development Research and Projects Centre (dRPC)
a4316.speech: Noted that with the withdrawal of key international donors like the US, UK, and EU—many of whom are redirecting funds to other priorities like national defence—Nigeria now faces a widening funding gap, and warned that these global aid reductions could have significant implications for the country’s reproductive health services, especially if domestic investment continues to decline.

a4316.speaker: Ijeoma Nwankwo, programme manager, Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria Foundation (PSNF)
a4316.speech: Expressed deep concern over the cut in Nigeria’s family planning budget, describing it as a major threat to reproductive health service delivery, especially in rural and underserved communities, and said the drastic reduction will significantly hinder access to essential family planning commodities and services for millions of women: “Without adequate funding, we risk reversing the progress made in reducing maternal mortality and improving women’s health outcomes.”

a4316.speaker: Ijeoma Nwankwo, programme manager, Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria Foundation (PSNF)
a4316.speech: Emphasised that while donor funding has historically supported Nigeria’s family planning initiatives, relying solely on external partners is not sustainable: “It’s time for the government, at all levels, to take ownership of reproductive health programmes. States must begin to allocate and release dedicated budgets for family planning as part of their commitment to primary health care and women’s health,” ; also highlighted the role of the private sector in bridging funding gaps, from strengthening supply chain systems to investing in public awareness campaigns and driving innovation around contraceptive access, and called on government to ensure continuity of family planning services nationwide.

a4316.speaker: Saleh Abba, family physician based in Borno State
a4316.speech: Recently disclosed in an interview that family planning uptake in Borno State dropped from 13,000 women in January to just 3,000 in February this year, and stated that the shortage of contraceptive supplies and the pause in donor funding are major reasons for this decline.

a4316.speaker: 2023 study published in BMC Women’s Health, “A narrative review of evidence to support increased domestic resource mobilisation for family planning in Nigeria”
a4316.speech: Emphasised the urgency of increasing domestic funding for family planning in Nigeria to ensure sustainability and reduce dependency on external donors, and found that heavy reliance on external donors makes funding for family planning services unpredictable and imbalanced.

a4316.speaker: UNFPA and the Guttmacher Institute (global estimates)
a4316.speech: Estimate that every dollar spent on family planning can save up to four dollars in maternal and newborn health costs.

a4316.speaker: Stanley Ilechukwu, executive director, South Saharan Social Development Organisation (SSDO)
a4316.speech: Noted that although the cessation of funding has thrown Nigeria’s health sector into disarray, there are still ways to mitigate the damage, and pointed out that the recent judicial stamp on the autonomy of Local Government Areas presents a unique opportunity: “With LGAs now ‘autonomous’, we should begin to hold them to the same standards as the federal and state governments and make them commit to the same pledges, particularly with regards to healthcare financing,” ; “It is critical to ensure that we are not just dependent on donor funding but are also creating domestic solutions to address these challenges.”

a4617.speaker: Travel agents
a4617.speech: Confirmed on Tuesday that the United Arab Emirates has introduced stricter visa regulations for Nigerian travellers, including a complete ban on transit visa applications ; say the toughened visa policy is expected to significantly curb travel from Nigeria to Dubai, which has long been a preferred destination for both business and leisure.

a4617.speaker: Dubai immigration authorities (notification)
a4617.speech: “For Nigerian nationals, please bear in mind that an applicant aged 18 to 45 years travelling alone is not eligible for the TOURIST VISA CATEGORY. An applicant who is 45 years or above must provide a Single Nigerian personal bank statement for a period of the last six months, with each month's end balance reflecting a minimum ending balance of USD 10,000 or its naira equivalent. Kindly note that the above points must be taken into consideration before sending your applications with other existing documents such as hotel reservation, data page, etc.”

a4617.speaker: U.S. Department of State
a4617.speech: Announced new restrictions affecting several countries, including Nigeria, and issued a statement on Tuesday saying the policy shift is expected to affect thousands of Nigerian students, businesspeople, tourists, and families who frequently travel to the U.S.: “Effective immediately, most non-immigrant and non-diplomatic visas issued to citizens of Nigeria will be single-entry visas with a three-month validity period.”

a4672.speaker: South African presidency (cabinet présidentiel)
a4672.speech: Said the discussions in Ireland will focus on strengthening bilateral cooperation between South Africa and Ireland in the fields of science, innovation, education and trade.

a4719.speaker: Sam Kutesa, Uganda's former Minister of Foreign Affairs and President of the UN General Assembly's 69th session
a4719.speech: Said, while attending the recent Africa Leadership Forum convened by the Uongozi Institute, that the Global Goals were the result of a process which was more inclusive, noting that prior to their approval, countries or governments around the world involved private businesses, civil society and public participation with local communities.

a4719.speaker: Sam Kutesa, Uganda's former Minister of Foreign Affairs and President of the UN General Assembly's 69th session
a4719.speech: Noted at the recently concluded 8th African Leadership Forum (ALF) in Kampala that the SDGs were well developed ambitions and that nothing was wrong with them, except that there is need to rethink financing models for the same; noted that the SDGs were proper aspirations and that what was needed for the continent is innovating new measures to finance their implementation, like leveraging local natural resources and the private sector to finance them.

a4719.speaker: Dr Jakaya Mrisho Kikwete, ALF 2025 convener, ALF Patron and fourth President of the United Republic of Tanzania
a4719.speech: Said there is need to reset SDGs implementation on the right path, with urgency of action and with high political will and turning ambition into action; noted that despite there being challenges in the implementation, that should be changed into opportunity and reaffirm local commitment to SDGs and Africa Agenda 2030; called for prioritizing of economic growth which then produces jobs and an education that is able to create world class learning outcomes and a middle class.

a4719.speaker: Hailemariam Desalegn, ALF co-convener and former Prime Minister of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia
a4719.speech: Noted that Africa faces opportunities but with challenges in achieving SDGs, such as a huge funding gap and thus significant resources needed to fill the gap; proposed alternatives to funding the SDGs while calling for solutions like strengthened governance and institutions, transparency, rule of law, combating corruption and curbing illicit financial flows, hand in hand with a resilient workforce, sustainable food security, reliable energy and strengthening of integration in trade and the broader economies across the continent through ceding some of individual countries' sovereignty and embracing the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA): "If it gets harder to trade with other more established economies in the west, its only prudent that we strengthen intra trade, leverage technology and innovation, resource mobilise and cur on foreign aid and Overseas Development Assistance (ODA)"

a4719.speaker: Antonio Pedro, Deputy Executive Secretary at the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa
a4719.speech: Noted that in implementing SDGs, it was important to understand that unemployment is not merely an economic concern but also a threat to peace and a test to our economic model, adding that the private sector must not just invest in profit but also in purpose; argued that the continent needed a recalibrated SDG model, further noting that removing tariff and non-tariff barriers has the potential to increase Africa's intra trade by 45 per cent in the next decade.

a4719.speaker: Mafa Chipeta, former FAO representative to Ethiopia, the African Union and UNECA, FAO Sub-regional Coordinator for Eastern Africa
a4719.speech: In a keynote statement, argued for an approach that is more selective and re-focused in implementation, noting that if the continent takes on all the SDGs at one go, it may spread itself too thin, hinging his argument on the facts that the continent has 17 to 18 percent of global population but with just 2 percent of the World GDP and trade, scores 3 percent for most economic indices and with only less than 0.5 percent for new critical technologies; cautioned that African trade ministries tend to ignore the larger domestic trade than foreign trade, which leaves exploitative traders to rob smallholders and continues to heavily subsidise the world economy by selling raw, unprocessed low value materials cheaply and buying the same back at inflated prices; proposed that the continent needs to cut down on donor dependency by still allocating its own funds so that donors don't replace local commitment.

a4719.speaker: Dr. Ernest Bai Koroma, former President of the Republic of Sierra Leone
a4719.speech: Noted that while the current 'America' first plan had created uncertainty in the rest of the world, it was also timely for Africa to grab this opportunity so that it re-anchors itself and makes new bold decisions in new development directions; urged prioritizing human capital development through education, health and social services delivery, agriculture development and good governance with leadership that is determined to drive all these processes.

a4973.speaker: Razak Kojo Opoku (PhD), Founding President of UP Tradition Institute (issued statement)
a4973.speech: Issued a statement setting out that the strategic vision of Dr Bryan Acheampong for the transformation of Ghana is anchored on three pillars: a "Development in Freedom" policy based on the political, economic, social, educational, cultural and international objectives of the 1992 Constitution and on fundamental human rights, media freedom and the supremacy of the Constitution; a business-friendly environment for the private sector and investors, including a massive drive for private sector growth, the promotion of Africapitalism, public-private partnerships at no cost to government, infrastructural development and a National Beautification Programme, and prudent management of the exchange rate, inflation and interest rates; and advancing Ghana's economic ecosystems through a well-diversified economy and massive investment in advanced technology, a Sustainable Digital Economic Revolution, sustainable food and agricultural products, sustainable energy supply, environmental sustainability addressing galamsey, and sustainable healthcare delivery across all MMDAs; concluded: "Ghana's Bright Future is with Bryan."

a4973.speaker: Dr Bryan Acheampong (DBA)
a4973.speech: Proposed the "No Region Left Behind Policy" for inclusive growth and inclusive development across Ghana, aimed at proper equitable national development.

a5209.speaker: Reports (cited on Gambian remittances)
a5209.speech: Reports show that remittances have come to contribute 20% in total from the GDP for The Gambia, where the majority of the funds are used for procuring household food items, requisite education and healthcare services.

a5215.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5215.speech: tweeted that “South Africa is confiscating land and maltreating certain classes.”

a5215.speaker: AfriForum
a5215.speech: has criticised the passing of the bill, calling it an evil and destructive agenda that can only harm South Africans ; called on the US to sanction the South African government and reverse the law.

a5215.speaker: Gwede Mantashe, South African Minister of Mineral and Petroleum Resources
a5215.speech: responded to these threats by calling Africa to unite against Trump by withholding minerals from the US.

a5387.speaker: Hadija Nakimuli, 62-year-old widowed shopkeeper at Owino market
a5387.speech: “Where is our future if they stop secondhand clothes?” the 62-year-old asked.

a5387.speaker: Kampala city authorities
a5387.speech: according to Kampala city authorities, the sprawling market employs some 80 000 people, 70 percent of them women.

a5387.speaker: Joseph Barimugaya, menswear stall holder at Owino market
a5387.speech: “Other than students, my clients include ministers (and) members of parliament who call me to deliver clothes to their air-conditioned offices” ; “This trade should not be tampered with. Everyone benefits, including the government, which gets taxes.”

a5387.speaker: Robert Twimukye, 27, teacher and Owino shopper
a5387.speech: “As a teacher I earn less than 500 000 Ugandan shillings. If I am to buy a new garment it means I would spend all my salary on clothing.”

a5387.speaker: Uganda Dealers in Used Clothings and Shoes Association
a5387.speech: estimates that 16 million people -- one in three Ugandans -- wear used clothing.

a5387.speaker: Allan Zavuga, retail manager of Think Twice
a5387.speech: “Everyone is into secondhand clothes. Only few people in Uganda can afford new clothes” ; “Banning it in Uganda is doing a disservice to the population and also the country at large,” he said, pointing out the environmental cost of producing new clothing instead of reusing items.

a5387.speaker: 2017 study by USAID, the US government’s aid agency
a5387.speech: East Africa imports about an eighth of the world’s used clothing, providing jobs for some 355 000 people who earn $230 million a year.

a5387.speaker: Yoweri Museveni, President of Uganda
a5387.speech: “These clothes are from the dead in a foreign country. When a white (person) dies, the clothes are sent to Africa” ; “I have declared war on secondhand clothes to promote African wear.”

a5387.speaker: David Bahati, Uganda’s state minister for trade
a5387.speech: said it was a question of “dignity” ; if the proposed ban goes ahead, “we will be able to replace these second hand clothes” ; “It cannot be done in one day but we can do it in a gradual manner” ; “The government is ready to give investors incentives... such as tax holidays to ensure we process our cotton into new garments to cover the market demands.”

a5387.speaker: Harriet Musoke Kyambadde, second-generation shopkeeper at Owino market
a5387.speech: “Who did the government consult (before deciding) to ban secondhand?” ; “Banning this business will be sending me into abject poverty.”

a5436.speaker: João Mosca, researcher at the Rural Observatory (OMR)
a5436.speech: Reveals that the displaced are involved in a corruption scheme, and denounces the government for preventing NGOs distributing support, a role which is allowed only to public institutions and the Army ; says that, for example, some displaced families are registering to receive help more than once, with the aim of diverting products into a corrupt trading scheme ; “The numbers of people officially designated displaced is higher than can possibly be, considering the population in Cabo Delgado... This means that people are registering at more than one site with their families in order to receive more food than they would receive in the case of individual families. The same family can register at several sites in order to receive two or three times more food than that which they would be entitled. Hence, a whole business process can be generated, which is already taking place among the displaced themselves.”

a5436.speaker: João Mosca, researcher at the Rural Observatory (OMR)
a5436.speech: On how the problem could be minimised: “Not only can it be [the case of] the same person registering at several sites, it can also be that people from the same family are registering at different sites. So, how to do it in these conditions is very difficult. However, locally I think that it would be possible if those distributing the resources pay more attention to those receiving it. And even among the community, they know very well who has the most resources and is trading in those goods. Only with local knowledge, being on the ground, but it must also be said that the people who distribute, the Army that does the distribution in some areas must be aware that they themselves must not enter into this business. Here, there is a multiplicity of interests and negotiations between people with different interests, who end up making commitments to each other, in the sense that we all win a little and we will make the most of it.”

a5436.speaker: João Mosca, researcher at the Rural Observatory (OMR)
a5436.speech: On international aid: “Mozambique has refused to allow international and national civil society organizations to distribute humanitarian assistance resources directly to the population. It means that the government requires that these resources be turned over to public institutions and the Army to carry out this distribution operation on the ground.”

a5436.speaker: João Mosca, researcher at the Rural Observatory (OMR)
a5436.speech: Asked whether this amounts to corruption in humanitarian aid in Cabo Delgado: “Absolutely. But not only on the part of the population, this type of business has been detected for some time. It is not unusual, because in other situations, for example, calamities, unfortunately very common in Mozambique, the public institutions themselves responsible for helping the population in conditions of strong environmental shocks, and now in a conflict situation, should be aware of the possibility of these phenomena appearing immediately in conditions of great instability and in places where displaced persons are hosted... It is a very generalised situation.”

a5457.speaker: Etienne Peterschmitt, FAO Representative in Somalia
a5457.speech: Lauded the agreement, stating, "This agreement is a major milestone in our efforts to improve food security in Somalia and provide a pathway from humanitarian assistance towards economic resilience. By sharing data, we can also be more efficient with our resources and move faster to support communities in crisis."

a5457.speaker: El-Khidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director for Somalia
a5457.speech: "As humanitarians we are committed to the principles of transparency and accountability to those that we serve. The digitization of assistance, and the secure sharing of data, will allow WFP and FAO to more effectively deliver life-saving and life-changing programmes to communities across Somalia."

a5515.speaker: Prince K. Moye, Bong County Senator (Liberia)
a5515.speech: Told journalists that rice produced from his farms will be bagged and sold for a reasonable price on the local market ; “We as leaders need to begin taking steps in making our country food sufficient. When public officials adopt these steps, it will greatly help the agriculture sector” ; told journalists that yield from his rice farm would be placed on the market for consumption as his way of contributing towards food security of Liberia.

a5515.speaker: Christopher Sankolo, Director General of the Liberia Agricultural Commodity Regulatory Authority (LACRA)
a5515.speech: Heaped praises on the lawmaker, describing him as a farsighted and development-oriented leader of Bong County; said the lawmaker’s action is worthy of commendation particularly at a time when the government is struggling to make Liberia food secure ; “Senator Moye has proven to be a national leader as demonstrated by his actions. I would like to appreciate him for his intervention as former National Campaigning Chairman of the Unity Party. This is welcoming.” ; said these are initiatives that demonstrate love for the country, adding “We hope that others will emulate what you are doing as we strive to make Liberia a food secure nation.”

a5515.speaker: Christopher Sankolo, Director General of LACRA
a5515.speech: Encouraged Senator Prince K. Moye to do intercropping, especially with cocoa and coffee, and encouraged Liberian farmers to get involved within the cocoa and coffee sector by investing in the sector.

a5515.speaker: 2021 Global Hunger Index (report)
a5515.speech: Classifies Liberia’s level of hunger as ‘serious’; Liberia ranked 110 of 116 countries on hunger conditions.

a5516.speaker: Josephine Adhet Deng, Advocate (complainant)
a5516.speech: Overtly accused Amb. Majur of criminal wrongdoing involving intimidation, defamation and sexual assault, and proceeded to issue an arrest warrant against Amb. Majur.

a5516.speaker: Josephine Adhet Deng, Advocate
a5516.speech: Lodged a case against a relative of Dr. Jok Madut Jok, whom she accused of having impregnated her stepdaughter ; filed a case against Dr. Jok, claiming that Dr. Jok’s right to bail out the accused young man was a criminal wrongdoing.

a5516.speaker: Josephine Adhet Deng, Advocate
a5516.speech: Had the artist Akuol Zakaria (aka Lady Kola) arrested on account of a preposterous claim that the artist composed a song titled “Little Girls” that promotes immorality.

a5516.speaker: Tong Deng Anei, author, former State Minister of Health of Northern Bahr el Ghazal State and former USAID/UN staffer
a5516.speech: “In my view, the underlying motive in this case appears to be the position occupied by Amb. Majur not because there is criminal wrongdoing by Amb. Majur.” ; appeals to the Prosecutor General to, first, strengthen South Sudan’s legal system by reviewing the work of public Attorneys under him, and secondly to ensure that those working under him are recruited based on a strong commitment to justice and public interest ; argues that Amb. Majur is entitled to sue both Advocate Adhet and the Office of the Prosecutor for wrongful use of public office and resources in pursuit of a personal vendetta.

a5516.speaker: Eye Radio (Editor’s Note)
a5516.speech: “The views expressed in the above article are solely those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of Eye Radio. All claims made are the author’s responsibility alone.”

a5954.speaker: Organisers of the seminar
a5954.speech: Observed that African countries in general and Benin in particular have for some decades been confronted with transnational organised crime.

a5954.speaker: Kevin Armstrong, Director of USAID Benin
a5954.speech: Pointed out that the training will make it possible to strengthen cooperation among the various actors in the fight and help lay the foundations for smooth communication among them; said he hopes that thanks to WACSI, civil society organisers will intensify awareness-raising and communicate with the public on issues linked to transnational organised crime, including corruption, so as to hold members of government and the authorities of State institutions accountable and bring them to ensure transparency and integrity in their respective sectors.

a5954.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Elias, President of FONAC (Front of National Organisations for the Fight against Corruption)
a5954.speech: Suggested that the seminar should bring about the mobilisation of national opinion on the threats posed by transnational organised crime to good governance and the economic development of the West African sub-region, and help lay the groundwork for good sub-regional cooperation between State and non-State actors in the fight.

a5954.speaker: Fortune Luc Olivier Guezo, Secretary General of the Ministry of Justice of Benin
a5954.speech: Assured that it could not be otherwise and suggested that the gravity of transnational organised crime and its impacts on the socio-economic development of nations require urgent and commensurate action to prevent and fiercely combat these scourges; judged it urgent to fight them through education, awareness-raising and training of actors, then to ensure application of the laws in force while emphasising international cooperation; indicated that the context of growing insecurity in the cities and at the borders calls for this, and reported that in recent years criminal activities have developed considerably, taking on a worrying scale marked by the diversification and rapid expansion of illicit activities, the increase in the number of countries affected, all supported by corruption.

a6159.speaker: Center for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD)
a6159.speech: Has called for the review of incentives that government has been providing to the mining sector because the output is not commensurate to what the country was putting in.

a6159.speaker: Isaac Mwaipopo, CTPD executive director
a6159.speech: Said government has provided a number of incentives to the mining sector but the way the sector had performed in the first half of 2023 leaves much to be desired ; Mr Mwaipopo said it would be very important that government relooks at some of the incentives that it has been providing to the mining sector and access the extent to which they were effective in stimulating the growth of the mining sector.

a6159.speaker: Center for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD)
a6159.speech: CTPD shared their reflection on the performance of the economy within the first half of 2023 which they indicated that Zambia's economy has encountered some challenges, the country was grappling with inflationary pressures, exchange rate fractions and the growth trajectory being hampered with downturns in key sectors such as Agriculture and Mining.

a6159.speaker: Elijah Mumba, lead researcher extractives, CTPD
a6159.speech: Said comparing what was happening in the mining sector in the first quarter of 2022 to the first quarter of 2023 there was a significant reduction in production by approximately 24 percent which was a serious concern.

a6247.speaker: Bishop Morris Banda, guest minister at the crusade
a6247.speech: Said they were excited to have Rose Muhando at the crusade: “Her music has touched countless lives and we believe her presence at the crusade will bring a new level of anointing and blessings to our gathering” ; called upon all believers to patronise the event, saying they would have three days of prayer, worship and spiritual transformation.

a6258.speaker: Several American media outlets
a6258.speech: Reported on Tuesday 15 April that the President is considering slashing half the State Department's budget, and that if the decision is approved by Congress, five consulates in France could close.

a6258.speaker: The Washington Post
a6258.speech: Revealed on 15 April an internal document showing the plan for massive budget cuts to American diplomacy, which had not been announced publicly; according to the newspaper, funding for the UN and NATO could cease, while certain organisations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency or the International Civil Aviation Organization could escape the cuts.

a6258.speaker: Memo of the White House Office of Management and Budget (internal document)
a6258.speech: Puts the State Department budget for fiscal year 2026 (starting October 2025) at $28.4 billion, a reduction of 48% compared with 2025; specifies that the budget for humanitarian aid should be cut by 54% and that for public health by 55%.

a6258.speaker: Punchbowl News
a6258.speech: Reported that the United States could close ten embassies and 17 consulates, notably in Eritrea, Luxembourg, South Sudan and Malta, and that five of the consulates threatened with closure would be in France, in Lyon, Rennes, Bordeaux, Strasbourg and Marseille.

a6258.speaker: Tammy Bruce, State Department spokesperson
a6258.speech: Gave no details, confining herself to recalling that no final decision has been taken for the time being.

a6258.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a6258.speech: Did not comment on the plan explicitly, but on Tuesday congratulated himself on X for having again “cancelled 139 grants worth $214 million.”

a6320.speaker: Unicef
a6320.speech: According to Unicef, food needs in the enclave are considerable and essential services have "collapsed" ; the scale of humanitarian needs for Gazans is "considerable"; the organisation explains that it expects to be able to reach "without hindrance all children and all families" in order to provide them with "the essential food and nutrition they need, but also health care, psychosocial support, drinking water, sanitation, education and learning services, as well as cash assistance" ; Unicef notes that of the 36 hospitals Gaza has, "less than half are still operational", a situation "that increases the risk of outbreaks of infectious diseases and puts children in danger".

a6320.speaker: Tom Fletcher, head of the UN Office for Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a6320.speech: Stressed: "After 15 months of war, humanitarian needs are staggering."

a6320.speaker: Jonathan Whittall, acting head of the UN humanitarian emergencies agency (OCHA) for the occupied Palestinian Territories
a6320.speech: Said the first humanitarian aid trucks entered Gaza a few minutes after the start of the ceasefire concluded between Israel and Hamas: "A massive effort has been deployed in recent days by humanitarian partners to load and prepare the distribution of massive aid throughout the Gaza Strip."

a6320.speaker: Egyptian official (anonymous)
a6320.speech: According to him, "260 aid trucks and 16 fuel trucks" entered via the Kerem Shalom crossing, between Israel and Gaza, and Nitzana, on the border between Egypt and Israel.

a6320.speaker: United Nations
a6320.speech: Has called on countries that have "influence" over Israel, Hamas and the armed gangs that loot convoys to use it so that the aid can indeed reach the population.

a6320.speaker: Tom Fletcher, head of the UN Office for Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a6320.speech: Wrote on X: "I urgently call on the countries that have some influence over all the parties to the agreement to ensure that this vital aid reaches those who need it most." ; "We are aware of the logistical challenges that exist for the people charged with delivering this aid, namely the mountains of rubble and the remnants of war that have not yet exploded. The safety of all our staff and of civilians remains our priority."

a6320.speaker: Unicef and the UN World Food Programme (WFP) (two statements)
a6320.speech: Also called for humanitarian actors to be able to "safely deploy the large-scale response that is sorely lacking within the Gaza Strip".

a6320.speaker: UN World Food Programme (WFP)
a6320.speech: Puts at 300 million dollars (about 290 million euros) the money needed to "meet the needs within the enclave for the next six months"; according to it, the war has left more than two million people "totally dependent" as regards their needs for food, housing and money; the WFP wishes to provide cash and vouchers to help 100,000 inhabitants.

a6320.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a6320.speech: Has estimated at "more than 10 billion dollars" the amount needed to put the health system back on its feet, judging the health challenges to be "immense".

a6537.speaker: Executive order signed by US President Donald Trump
a6537.speech: The order stated: “All department and agency heads with responsibility for United States foreign development assistance programmes should immediately pause new obligations and disbursements of development assistance funds.”

a6537.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a6537.speech: At the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations in 2018, complained that the United States was the biggest donor of foreign aid but that only a few give anything in return: “That is why we are taking a hard look at United States foreign assistance. Moving forward, we will only provide foreign aid to those who respect us and, frankly, are our friends.”

a6643.speaker: Nigerien traders and economists
a6643.speech: Supported the decision, considering it a "logical" measure for the junta-led countries given that their relations with ECOWAS have deteriorated in recent years.

a6675.speaker: Armindo Tiago, Mozambican Minister of Health, and Dennis Hearne, United States Ambassador to Mozambique
a6675.speech: During today's handover event at the U.S. Government-funded Central Medical Stores (CMAM) warehouse in Zimpeto, Minister Tiago and Ambassador Hearne spoke of the longstanding partnership between the two countries.

a6675.speaker: Dennis Hearne, United States Ambassador to Mozambique
a6675.speech: "Today's ventilator donation builds on the nearly $14.8 million in U.S. funds supporting COVID-19 efforts in Mozambique. We have donated personal protective equipment, known as PPE (Personal Protective Equipment), and we have worked together on challenges such as water and sanitation, emergency food assistance, infection prevention and control, and much more."

a6712.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a6712.speech: Is sounding the alarm that nearly 29 million people in six Sahel countries will need humanitarian assistance and protection in 2025.

a6712.speaker: OCHA humanitarian needs overview for the Sahel region (report)
a6712.speech: According to the latest humanitarian needs overview for the region, $4.3 billion is needed to assist 18.4 million people in Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad, Mali, Niger, and Nigeria.

a6712.speaker: Charles Bernimolin, OCHA's Regional Director for West and Central Africa
a6712.speech: "Millions of vulnerable women, children, and men are in emergency situations." ; "Without adequate funding, lives will be lost." ; warned "This is not about budget figures, it's about human lives. Inaction will be costly", calling for urgent donor mobilisation.

a6714.speaker: National Peace Council (NPC) of Ghana
a6714.speech: Said it was hopeful of a smooth transition process following the successful conduct of the 2024 general election because systems had been put in place for that.

a6714.speaker: Rev. Dr Ernest Adu-Gyamfi, Chairman of the National Peace Council
a6714.speech: "I'm hopeful that between now and January 7, they should be able to clear whatever needs to be done and then we should have a smooth process." ; said the Peace Council had always been part of the election and so in between the transitional period, if there was any need for it to play a role again, it would do so to ensure that the country remained peaceful and stable.

a6714.speaker: Rev. Dr Ernest Adu-Gyamfi, Chairman of the National Peace Council
a6714.speech: Said the council was aware that a lot of things had been done already: "The current government has put in place measures to ensure the process is smooth. Yes, we are aware that a lot of things have been done. Before the elections, most of the ministries and others were asked to start writing their handover notes." ; urged all to allow the system that had been put in place to work to ensure a seamless process.

a6714.speaker: Rev. Dr Ernest Adu-Gyamfi, Chairman of the National Peace Council
a6714.speech: Advised sections of the youth engaging in acts of violence and looting following the declaration of the election outcomes to put a stop to it.

a6714.speaker: Electoral Commission of Ghana (official declaration)
a6714.speech: Declared the flag bearer of the National Democratic Congress, John Dramani Mahama, winner of the 2024 presidential election; per the results declared from 267 constituencies, excluding nine constituencies, Mr Mahama polled 6,328,397 votes, representing 56.55 per cent of the valid votes cast, while Dr Bawumia got 4,657,304 votes, representing 41.61 per cent.

a6836.speaker: Colonel Elhadj Ousmane Mahaman, Minister of Agriculture and Livestock of Niger
a6836.speech: Expressed his gratitude to the American government, whose continued commitment and support to Niger are invaluable; said that through USAID the United States has supported initiatives touching on vital areas such as food, health, education, governance and community resilience in the face of shocks and crises, and added that this partnership reflects USAID's long-standing commitment to supporting Niger in its ambition for sustainable and inclusive development towards absolute sovereignty.

a6836.speaker: Colonel Elhadj Ousmane Mahaman, Minister of Agriculture and Livestock of Niger
a6836.speech: Said that questions of food, health, education, crisis and disaster management and good governance are at the centre of the priorities of the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland (CNSP): “Convinced that the stability and development of our country rest on solid foundations of sustainable agricultural production and nutritional security, your approach will without any doubt contribute to the empowerment of local populations specifically, but also to food and nutritional sovereignty overall. That is why we welcome the advances of the HAMZARI programme, which has managed to combine concrete actions promoting agriculture, livestock farming and nutrition, contributing to integrated and sustainable development.”

a6836.speaker: Colonel Elhadj Ousmane Mahaman, Minister of Agriculture and Livestock of Niger
a6836.speech: Specified that the actions of the HAMZARI programme have directly reached 104,986 people, 62% of them women; urged participants to contribute actively to the workshop sessions, discussions and group work, to share their experiences and expertise, and to contribute fully to developing innovative and effective solutions to lay the groundwork for sustaining the gains: “Together, we can make a real difference for Niger, by ensuring healthy food for the population and improving the quality of life of our most vulnerable people.”

a6836.speaker: Maria Barron, USAID Niger Mission Director
a6836.speech: Recalled that the resilience and food security of communities have always been a priority for USAID in Niger, and that through its humanitarian assistance bureau USAID has funded resilience and food security projects since 2008 without any interruption: “USAID is determined to support the government of Niger in strengthening the resilience of communities in the face of crises. We are convinced that, thanks to strong partnerships and an approach centred on innovation and inclusion, we can continue to build a future in which every Nigerien can live in dignity, with access to essential services, sustainable livelihoods and a secure environment.”

a6836.speaker: Maria Barron, USAID Niger Mission Director
a6836.speech: Noted that since 2018 USAID has invested 195 million dollars (about 118 billion CFA francs) over a seven-year priority period in the Maradi and Zinder regions through three programmes — Hamzari, Wadata and Girma — specifically intended to strengthen resilience in Niger, in addition to other investments in agriculture, health, education and emergency humanitarian assistance, and that by the end of their implementation the three programmes will have reached nearly 2 million people; indicated that after six years of implementation Hamzari has achieved important results, with more than 17,000 farmers learning and applying improved production techniques and more than 58,000 people gaining better access to drinking water.

a6836.speaker: Maria Barron, USAID Niger Mission Director
a6836.speech: Reiterated USAID's unwavering and continued commitment to supporting the communities of Niger: “As the American government, we will remain at the side of the Nigerien people, working together for food security and a resilient and prosperous future for Niger.”

a6836.speaker: Yawo Douvon, Country Director of Care
a6836.speech: Specified that his organisation's engagement in Niger and Burkina is deployed through four major programmatic priorities — gender justice, economic justice, humanitarian assistance, and food and nutritional security and adaptation to climate change — and that the Hamzari programme particularly embodies this last priority; assured that Care will continue to work resolutely and in solidarity to support the government of Niger in achieving its sustainable development and resilience objectives: “I want to express all my gratitude to the participating Hamzari communities for their determination and commitment, which have made these results possible.”

a6836.speaker: Yawo Douvon, Country Director of Care
a6836.speech: Recalled that in six years of implementation the Hamzari programme has directly reached more than 104,000 people, 62% of them women, thus attaining 106% of its initial target, and that the progress achieved in agriculture, livestock farming, nutrition and access to water is remarkable; reaffirmed Care's commitment to Niger's most vulnerable populations: “We will continue to work for inclusive, equitable and sustainable development by placing gender justice, economic empowerment, food security and resilience at the heart of our actions.”

a6910.speaker: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) report, "COVID-19 Human Development, Exploring Global Preparedness & Vulnerability"
a6910.speech: Demonstrates that the impact of the Novel Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic will be felt throughout every aspect of society ; underscores that there are different factors that determine the overall preparedness and vulnerability of countries and regions to the ramifications of the virus, listing three main categories to assess how prepared and equipped a country or region is: its Human Development Index (HDI), its health system, and connectivity ; in its second data set details which countries are more vulnerable than others due to pre-existing conditions, using indicators such as the percentage of the population living below the poverty line and immediate economic vulnerability.

a6910.speaker: Nuhamin Petros, PhD student in epidemiology at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden
a6910.speech: Said that during a pandemic countries rely on their health resources and can use such data to pinpoint where much more work is needed: "By analysing and predicting areas that can be particularly affected by the virus, governments can determine where the involvement of the community is crucial, especially in countries like Ethiopia where community engagement is very much a necessity" ; "An additional benefit is the lessons learned that identify strategies if anything similar comes into play."

a6910.speaker: Tsegaye Gebrekidan (PhD), economist at the Policy Studies Institute
a6910.speech: Said the preparedness and vulnerability of nations vary and so the report is critical in developing a response plan suited to the country's needs: "In a country like Ethiopia, where the preparedness indicators show a lack of resources, there needs to be a focus on prevention and containment strategies such as the ones we are using."

a6910.speaker: Tsegaye Gebrekidan (PhD), economist at the Policy Studies Institute
a6910.speech: Said that even in partial lockdown the economy is still suffering, that the country does not have a buffer for the economic impact and that governments may not have the capacity to deal with it single-handedly, so donors are also essential in this fight ; "Beyond helping us realise what kind of economic response a country should craft, this data can also help when requesting assistance from donors in specific areas."

a6910.speaker: Ministry of Finance (Ethiopia)
a6910.speech: Said remittances, already reduced by 30pc between January and March, might fall further to 75pc in the period between February and June.

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria' and Nigeria's Ambassador
a6945.speech: Said that in spite of the demanding nature of his diplomatic job he made out time at weekends and during holidays to write the book, and that even though he lost the original manuscript he remained determined and started writing afresh.

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria'
a6945.speech: Stated his motivations for writing the book: that he was driven by patriotic zeal to contribute to knowledge about the security problems facing his country, and (at p.34) that he wanted to help in boosting better understanding of the phenomenon of Boko Haram and related security issues of banditry and kidnappings, especially in Northern Nigeria, with information.

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria'
a6945.speech: Declared in his letter inviting the reviewer to review the book that the proceeds from the event would be used by his Foundation 'towards humanitarian assistance to victims of Boko Haram and other violent conflicts in Nigeria.'

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria'
a6945.speech: Notes that Boko Haram was formed in 2002 by Mohammed Yusuf, although other accounts suggested that it was formed earlier by other persons.

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria'
a6945.speech: Found that Boko Haram was 'homegrown' and grew out of the fertile ground of Borno State as the epicentre before spreading to other parts of the country; in his view the phenomenon could have been nipped in the bud if only government had heeded intelligence reports and advice of well-meaning individuals and recommendations of committees set up by government at the initial stages, but elements of disbelief and concocted 'conspiracy theories' fouled the air, leading to a tragic miscomprehension of the Boko Haram phenomenon and failure to face the situation squarely.

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria'
a6945.speech: Noted that several other security challenges, namely kidnappings, banditry, communal clashes and violent separatist tendencies, existed before the emergence of Boko Haram, but that these crises assumed greater and sinister complexities after the manifestation of the Boko Haram terrorism which turned into an insurgency.

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria'
a6945.speech: Identifies the components of the security challenges nationwide as the products of bad governance, some of the challenges dating back to colonial times, and of a lack of proper appreciation of the problems and of addressing their root causes, with bad governance manifested in acts of corruption such as outright embezzlement and misappropriation of public funds; lists other causative factors fuelling terrorism, insurgency and kidnapping as drugs, indoctrination, fundamentalism, guns and human trafficking, hate culture, religion, revenge, ideology, poverty arising mainly from lack of job opportunities, illiteracy, living environment, corruption characterised by bad governance and lack of political will, and foreign dimensions.

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria'
a6945.speech: Acknowledged that poverty cannot be the sole push factor for engaging in acts of terrorism, citing ample examples in other parts of the world where people got involved in terrorism to promote some causes or ideological beliefs, while noting that poverty, unemployment and illiteracy worsened by unbearable living conditions may generate protests and render individuals easily recruited into terror and kidnapping cells.

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria'
