a6945.speech: Discussed the foreign dimensions of Boko Haram's activities from two broad perspectives, stating that from Boko Haram's perspective there was sufficient evidence from pronouncements of leading personalities, video recordings and debriefings to show that Boko Haram forged alliances with like-minded outside groups that offered logistics, personnel, finance and training facilities, and that logos and designation of certain places of operation with foreign names were clear signatures of foreign connections and involvement.

a6945.speaker: Abdullahi Y. Shehu, author of 'Boko Haram and other Security Challenges in Nigeria'
a6945.speech: Observed that the Nigerian Government did not press hard for international support from outside the immediate neighboring countries bordering the theatre of the war against the insurgency, and gathered that when trouble broke out somewhere in Europe, those powers' attention was diverted to where their hegemonic interests were at more perilous stake.

a6945.speaker: Nigerian Government
a6945.speech: Declared in 2018 that Boko Haram had been 'technically defeated'; had misgivings that some of the external humanitarian supports received were being used as a cover for some sinister motives.

a7006.speaker: Epiphane Gilderic Adjovi, economist
a7006.speech: Said the resurgence of protectionism by the United States since President Donald Trump's return to power constitutes a major economic event, and that the decision can be considered a calling into question of the tariff preference granted by the United States to certain countries, including Benin, through AGOA; although the share of the United States in Benin's exports is still fairly low (a little less than 2% between 2021 and 2023), it shows a very marked upward trend; "The abandonment of AGOA and the imposition of a 10% customs duty will inevitably lead to increased competition for the products we export to that country. This may contribute to a reduction in our exports to the United States. The consequence must be a worsening of the deficit in Benin's trade balance, which is structurally in deficit."

a7006.speaker: Epiphane Gilderic Adjovi, economist
a7006.speech: Said that despite the relative weakness of the share of Beninese products sold on the American market, the measure could have notable repercussions on several macroeconomic indicators: "one can expect a contraction of investment in sectors oriented towards exporting to the United States, a fall in the incomes of the producers concerned, as well as a decrease in the volume of goods transiting through Benin bound for the American market," which could also negatively affect the country's port activities.

a7006.speaker: Epiphane Gilderic Adjovi, economist
a7006.speech: Said it is too early to have a precise estimate of the impact on the textile factories installed at the Glo-Djigbe Industrial Zone (Gdiz), but that since conquering the American market is among the investors' objectives there is a risk of a slowdown in foreign investment, while adequate trade facilitation measures could improve competitiveness and attract investors; "From my point of view, the situation should not be dramatised... our capacity to react can spare our economy a significant slowdown in its rate of growth."

a7006.speaker: Epiphane Gilderic Adjovi, economist
a7006.speech: Argued that the response must not be limited to seeking a short-term readjustment, since obtaining new unilateral preferences through bilateral renegotiation would always expose Benin to an abrupt reversal in the future; urged continuation of the policy of diversifying export products and markets and the elimination of all practices and measures that obstruct competitiveness, saying such an option should make the country more resilient to the trade policy shocks of its partners.

a7006.speaker: Epiphane Gilderic Adjovi, economist
a7006.speech: Said the question of AGOA's fate remains entirely open since the United States has taken measures, since President Trump's return, suggesting it is no longer in a logic of special and differentiated treatment for developing countries: "I am referring to the suspension of the programmes managed by USAID. In my opinion, as to the fate that will be reserved for AGOA until September 2025, clarifications must be given by the American side." Said what is most worrying is what happens to the instrument after September 2025, and proposed that the authorities assume AGOA will not be renewed and begin taking measures so as not to be excluded from the American market because of the lack of competitiveness of Beninese products.

a7006.speaker: Epiphane Gilderic Adjovi, economist
a7006.speech: Argued that shocks of this nature create the conditions for a readjustment of economic strategies and that countries must avoid building an entire strategy on preferential agreements; said it is now time to put in place strategies for improving the competitiveness of export products and to diversify export destinations, relying on other mechanisms such as the AfCFTA, which "should allow us to have better access to the African market"; added that Benin's membership of regional organisations such as WAEMU, ECOWAS and the AU requires a concerted approach in trade policy, and that the regional approach increases negotiating power, "which, even at that scale, is still very weak."

a7138.speaker: Eritrean nationals in the diaspora (at Martyrs' Day commemoration events)
a7138.speech: Participated in programs that included speeches focusing on the deep meaning of the day to the Eritrean people, as well as the responsibility of nationals to support the families of martyrs ; nationals also pledged to assume greater responsibility in supporting the families of martyrs.

a7138.speaker: Reports (cited)
a7138.speech: According to reports, nationals in the US cities of Las Vegas and Raleigh-Durham; in the UK cities of London, Sheffield, Leicester, Newcastle, Liverpool, Nottingham, Coventry, Bristol, Cardiff, Wakefield, Middlesbrough, Southampton, Glasgow, Birmingham, Manchester, Leeds, and Brighton; in the Saudi cities of Riyadh, Jeddah, and Al-Namas; as well as in the Angolan cities of Benguela, Lubango, Huambo, Cabinda, Lucapa, have commemorated Martyrs' Day with candlelight vigils and cultural and artistic programs in remembrance of Eritrean martyrs who sacrificed their lives for independence and national sovereignty.

a7359.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a7359.speech: reflected on the country’s progress since independence and outlined his vision for the future. He said the celebration was a reminder of the nation’s struggles for freedom and self-rule: “It reinforces our national identity, our unity and patriotism while offering a moment for reflection on our progress and the challenges ahead.”

a7359.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a7359.speech: said it would have been “unconscionable” to spend GH¢20 million on the celebrations as was done in the past considering the nation’s ongoing economic crisis: “This is necessary, considering the economic crisis our nation is currently experiencing. Large-scale celebrations often come with significant security and infrastructure costs, which strain the national budget” ; “By reducing the scale of the commitment, we wish to demonstrate a commitment to fiscal responsibility and the efficient use of our limited resources.”

a7359.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a7359.speech: pledged to provide “bold leadership and the clarity of vision that is needed to navigate the turbulent economic waters we are sailing in currently while safeguarding our future”.

a7359.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a7359.speech: emphasised the need for the country to break free from its cycle of dependence on foreign aid, stressing that proclaiming self-reliance while relying on donors was meaningless.

a7359.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a7359.speech: said a $10 billion initiative to modernise the country’s infrastructure, create jobs and stimulate local industry was underway.

a7522.speaker: Kathérine Overcamp, CRS Resident Representative in Benin
a7522.speech: Indicates that the project, focused on peacebuilding and conflict prevention, is implemented by CRS thanks to the generosity of the American people through USAID, and will be deployed over a 24-month period covering 4 communes — Parakou and Tchaourou in Borgou, and Bantè and Savè in Collines — targeting traditional, political and religious leaders, young people, women and marginalised groups, aiming to directly impact 6,795 participants and 33,975 indirectly. ; Explains that the start-up activities begun in March 2023 made it possible, by the end of October 2023, to strengthen the capacities of the project implementation teams on the different implementation approaches, notably the social cohesion approach known as 3B/4D, peaceful masculinity, and conflict prevention and management: "We estimate at 191 the number of actors and authorities already trained who have committed to peacebuilding activities. 639 women, young people and other vulnerable persons have also joined 29 savings and credit community groups out of the 96 groups planned."

a7522.speaker: Simon Asoba, USAID political adviser, speaking on behalf of the US Ambassador to Benin
a7522.speech: Wishing great success to the project, observes that in the face of recent challenges and the rise of insecurity in northern Benin, these actions are to be welcomed and encouraged: "I had the opportunity to see the progress made in the localities of Karo, Nikki Kpérou, Sanson and in the Yarakinnin neighbourhood in Parakou, and I was impressed by the commitment of the notables, men and women, determined to work together for a community of peace but also to organise themselves to mobilise internal savings on their own for their own prosperity." ; Specifies that the project, led by CRS and its partners Caritas Parakou and Caritas Dassa, is an example of USAID's commitment in northern and central Benin, with total funding of 620,000,000 CFA francs.

a7522.speaker: Djibril Mama Cissé, prefect of the department of Borgou
a7522.speech: Welcomes this initiative led by CRS, which is in perfect alignment with the government's action programme under its pillar 1, "Strengthening democracy, the rule of law and good governance", and fits with the Sustainable Development Goals: "I would like to assure you of the commitment of my colleague the prefect of Collines, of the mayors, of the beneficiary communes and myself, to support the implementation of the project so that it truly impacts the beneficiaries."

a7522.speaker: Saliou Odoubou, prefect of the department of Collines
a7522.speech: Welcomes the relevance of the project, embracing the assertion of Jean Jaurès: "Today, the affirmation of peace is the greatest of struggles", before expressing the wish that through this project, the coexistence for which the two departments, and Benin in general, are recognised may be strengthened.

a7522.speaker: Dénis Oba Chabi, mayor of the commune of Savè
a7522.speech: Says this project comes at just the right time, especially after the electoral violence of recent years, to explain to everyone the necessity and the obligation of living together, in peace, in total cohesion. "It is in everyone's interest," he added.
